The boy is not allowed to go out.
negatives: The machine wasn't fixed properly.
He does not accept the terms.

can_do_statement: Can form the 'get'-passive with a range of forms of 'get' + past participles.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'get' with a past participle to describe things that happen to someone, often accidentally.

positives: mine got broken, so I need it to see myself in it.
You should be careful while you are crossing or you will get hurt.
negatives: I got a nice present.
She has got red hair.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past continuous questions.

positives: What were you doing there?
Was he playing with you?
negatives: He was playing with you.
I was not doing anything.

can_do_statement: Can use the past continuous with an increasing range of adverbs in the normal mid position.

ontology.mental_model: Modifying past ongoing action with diverse adverbs.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past continuous + actually/still/suddenly.

positives: He was still waiting for her.
She was actually acting like a ghost.
negatives: I was just waiting.
I was always dreaming.

can_do_statement: Can use the past continuous to give a reason for something, often with 'because'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Because + past continuous.

positives: I stayed home because it was raining.
Because she was sitting there, she saw him.
negatives: It was raining heavily.
I went home because it rained.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past continuous negative.

positives: He was not planning to go.
Her phone wasn't working.
negatives: He was planning to go.
I am not planning to go.

can_do_statement: Can use the past continuous to talk about ongoing repeated events in the past, often with 'always'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past continuous + always

positives: He was always talking during the lecture.
They were always complaining about the weather.
negatives: He is always talking during the lecture.
She always talked about him.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect continuous talk about a background action or event which began before a point in the past and was still continuing up to a point in the past when the main event happened.

ontology.mental_model: Past perfect continuous for background events
ontology.pedagogical_hook: had been doing before something happened

positives: I had been walking for hours when I finally found the cabin.
They'd been trying to fix the car before they called a mechanic.
negatives: I have been walking for hours.
They had fixed the car.

can_do_statement: Can use the affirmative form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: had been doing

positives: I had been studying all night.
We'd been planning the trip for months.
negatives: I hadn't been studying all night.
We have been planning the trip.

guideword: USE: CONTINUING EVENTS IN THE PAST
can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect continuous to talk about an action or event which began before a point in the past and was still continuing up to that point, often with 'for' or 'since', to give background information.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: had been doing for/since

positives: They had been living there for five years.
She had been waiting since three o'clock.
negatives: They had been living there until recently.
They have been living there for five years.

can_do_statement: Can use negative forms.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: had not done

positives: Our company had not delivered the goods on time.
I hadn't heard from her for two months.
negatives: Our company had delivered the goods on time.
I hadn't been hearing from her for two months.

can_do_statement: Can use the affirmative form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: had done

positives: I felt really sorry for you after I had read your last letter.
I'd forgotten that I had an appointment.
negatives: I had not read your last letter.
I had been reading your last letter.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect simple with a limited range of adverbs (including 'never', 'ever', 'just', 'always', 'already') in the normal mid-position. ► adverbs

ontology.mental_model: Past perfect simple with mid-position adverbs
ontology.pedagogical_hook: had never/ever/just/always/already done

positives: It was the most beautiful one I had ever seen.
I had just arrived from school when I saw the letter.
negatives: It was the most beautiful one I have ever seen.
I had really loved the beautiful one I saw.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect simple in 'if'-clauses to talk about imagined situations in the past, often with regret. ► 'if'-clauses

ontology.mental_model: Past perfect simple in 3rd conditional if-clauses
ontology.pedagogical_hook: if ... had done

positives: If the weather had been better, we would have enjoyed it more.
If you had gone there with me, you would have been happy.
negatives: The weather had been better.
If you go there with me, you will be happy.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect simple to talk about a time before another time in the past.

ontology.mental_model: Sequencing a past action before another past point
ontology.pedagogical_hook: The "past in the past" for narrative timeline building

positives: He then thought how stupid he had been.
Actually I'd arranged an appointment with my doctor before calling you.
negatives: I have arranged a meeting for tomorrow.
She had a really great time at the party.

can_do_statement: Can use the affirmative form with a wide range of verbs.

ontology.mental_model: Action completed at a specific time in the past.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past simple affirmative applied to diverse verbs.

positives: I convinced some of my friends to come with me.
The cameraman suddenly filmed us during a lesson.
negatives: I convince some of my friends to come.
The cameraman is filming us.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form with an increasing range of verbs.

ontology.mental_model: Stating that a past event did not happen.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'did not' or 'didn't' to form negative past statements.

positives: I didn't realise I had lost the ring.
We had one in the garage that we did not immediately use.
negatives: I don't realise I have lost the ring.
We have one in the garage that we do not use.

can_do_statement: Can use the past simple to talk about habitual states or actions.

ontology.mental_model: A recurrent event or state in the past that is no longer happening.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past simple used with adverbs of frequency.

positives: He always seemed so confident to me.
We often talked during the class.
negatives: He always seems so confident to me.
We often talk during the class.

can_do_statement: Can use the past simple to order sequences of events in the past, in the context of narratives.

ontology.mental_model: Narrating a series of sequential events in the past.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'and' or 'and then' to link multiple past actions.

positives: He met a lot of new friends, and then got married.
We met at 9 and decided to go.
negatives: He meets a lot of friends and then gets married.
We meet at 9 and decide to go.

can_do_statement: Can use the past simple with 'wish (that)' to express regret that things are not different.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing desire for a present or future situation to be different.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'wish' followed by the past simple.

positives: I wish that you were here.
I wish weekends lasted five days.
negatives: I wish you the best of luck.
They wish to speak to you.

can_do_statement: Can use the past simple after 'if' to talk about the possible result of an imagined situation in the present or future.

ontology.mental_model: Hypothesizing about unreal or unlikely present/future conditions.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using the past simple after 'if' to imagine alternatives.

positives: If you wanted to do some activities, we could go.
It would be better if you spent some time here.
negatives: If you want to do some activities, we can go.
It will be better if you spend some time.

can_do_statement: Can use 'yes/no', 'wh-', tag and negative question forms with a limited range of verbs.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'did' or 'didn't' to form a question.

positives: Did you receive my present?
Why didn't he call me?
negatives: Do you receive my present?
Why doesn't he call me?

can_do_statement: Can use the question form with a limited range of verbs.

ontology.mental_model: Inquiring about ongoing actions up to the present.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'have/has' + 'been' + verb-ing in a question.

positives: Have you been thinking about it a lot?
What have you been doing?
negatives: Are you thinking about it a lot?
What were you doing?

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect continuous to talk about repeated activities which began in the past and are still continuing.

ontology.mental_model: An ongoing activity that started in the past and continues or has just finished.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect continuous structure: have/has been + verb-ing.

positives: I've been watching TV a lot lately.
He has been going there for two weeks.
negatives: I am watching TV a lot.
He had been going there for two weeks.

can_do_statement: Can use the affirmative form.

ontology.mental_model: An ongoing activity that started in the past and continues.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect continuous structure: have/has been + verb-ing.

positives: We've been studying together since grade one.
I have recently been thinking about your letter.
negatives: We are studying together.
I had been thinking about your letter.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect continuous to talk about a single activity or state that began in the past and is still continuing, often with 'for' or 'since'.

ontology.mental_model: Action began in past and continues to present
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect continuous for single continuing event with for/since

positives: I have been studying French since I was a child.
She has been living there for three years now.
negatives: I have been to Paris before.
They are studying for their exam.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect simple with 'already' to emphasise that something is done, often before the expected time.  ► adverbs

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect simple with 'already'

positives: I have already planned the trip.
She has already spoken to the manager.
negatives: I will already be there.
They haven't done it yet.

can_do_statement: Can use the affirmative forms with a range of pronouns and nouns and an increasing range of verbs.

ontology.mental_model: Reporting positive past events connected to present state
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect simple affirmative

positives: She has signed the contract.
We've moved to a new city.
negatives: I haven't signed anything.
He has never seen snow.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative forms with a range of pronouns and an increasing range of verbs.

ontology.mental_model: Denial of past events connected to present
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect simple negative forms

positives: He hasn't spoken to anyone.
We have not decided where to go.
negatives: I have decided already.
They didn't go to the park.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect simple with 'since' to talk about duration.

ontology.mental_model: Marking the starting point of a continuous state
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect simple with 'since'

positives: I have lived here since 2005.
It's been a long time since we met.
negatives: I lived here since I was born.
She was working there.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative question form.

ontology.mental_model: Seeking confirmation of an expected event
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Negative present perfect simple questions

positives: Haven't you seen the new update?
Hasn't he given you the money?
negatives: Have you seen the new update?
Why haven't they left yet?

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect simple to refer to a finished event or state in the recent past, that has a present relevance, often with 'just'.  ► adverbs

ontology.mental_model: Past events that have just finished with present relevance.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: When talking about something that happened very recently, use 'have/has just' plus the past participle.

positives: I've just received your mail.
My mother has just broken her right leg.
negatives: I just received your mail.
I'm just going to the shop.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect simple with an increasing range of adverbs in the normal mid position.

ontology.mental_model: Placing adverbs smoothly between the auxiliary 'have' and the main verb in present perfect tense.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Adverbs like 'always', 'never', 'already' go right after 'have' or 'has' in present perfect sentences.

positives: I've always loved seafood.
She has never seen this movie.
negatives: I always love seafood.
She never saw this movie.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect simple to refer to a state or period of time which is unlimited or indefinite.

ontology.mental_model: Describing states or situations that started in the past and continue into the present.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use the present perfect with stative verbs to talk about something true from the past until now.

positives: I've known him for years.
It has been a sunny, warm weekend.
negatives: I know him very well.
It was a sunny, warm weekend.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect simple with a superlative adjective to talk about a unique experience.  ► adjectives: superlatives

ontology.mental_model: Connecting a subjective ultimate evaluation to the total experience up to now.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: When you say something is the 'best' or 'most', you often use the present perfect with 'ever' to describe your experience.

positives: This restaurant has the most delicious shrimps I have ever tasted.
That is the best game I've played.
negatives: I have played a very good game.
This is the best game I play.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of simple (single word) prepositions.

ontology.mental_model: Spatial, temporal, and abstract relationship markers
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using a wider variety of single-word prepositions to convey specific abstract or physical relationships.

positives: We walked along the beautiful beach.
I think the city won't change that much within the next twenty years.
negatives: I went to the store yesterday.
She is sitting on the big chair.

can_do_statement: Can end a reported question clause and a relative clause with a preposition, where the preposition is stranded from its complement. ► Clauses: relative

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Leaving the preposition at the end of the clause when its object has been moved to the front (e.g., in relative clauses).

positives: This is the best festival I have been to.
Please give him all the information he asks for.
negatives: I went to the beautiful store.
He works for a very large company.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of complex prepositions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Combining adverbs, adjectives, or nouns with simple prepositions to form complex relationship markers.

positives: I want to play tennis instead of football.
The game was cancelled due to the heavy rain.
negatives: I have an interesting book about ancient history.
He was playing a brand new video game.

can_do_statement: Can use adverbs of degree to modify prepositions and prepositional phrases.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using degree adverbs precisely before prepositions to emphasize or modify the exactness of the location or relationship.

positives: I am going to put it right in front of the window.
It is quite near my house so I can go there.
negatives: I really like playing tennis with my friends.
He was quite happy about the entire situation.

can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous to describe temporary actions which are repeated or regular.

ontology.mental_model: Repeated events within a limited timeframe
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using continuous forms of typically stative or enduring verbs like 'have' or 'take' to frame habitual actions as temporary.

positives: I am having some complicated problems with my car.
I am currently taking a Spanish language class.
negatives: I have a brand new silver car.
He is making a big chocolate cake.

can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous with a wide range of verbs to talk about temporary situations.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present continuous for temporary situations

positives: I am currently studying in London for the summer.
They are staying at a nice hotel this week.
negatives: I studied in London last year.
They stay at that hotel every summer.

can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous with a wide range of verbs to talk about situations and events in progress.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present continuous for events happening now

positives: I am planning a big party for my brother.
We are getting very close to the final decision.
negatives: I plan to go there tomorrow.
We get a new car every five years.

can_do_statement: Can use 'don't you think' or 'don't you agree' to look for agreement or an opinion.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Negative tag questions

positives: It is a bit strange, don't you think?
That is the best way, don't you agree?
negatives: Do you think it is strange?
I don't agree with you on that.

can_do_statement: Can use 'yes/no' and 'wh-' question forms with a wide range of subjects.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present simple questions

positives: Does your brother go with your parents?
Where do they want to spend their holidays?
negatives: He does not want to go there.
Are they going on holiday soon?

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple with an increasing a range of mental process verbs, including 'remember', 'understand', 'believe'.

ontology.mental_model: Expression of memory, understanding, or belief
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Mental process verbs (remember, understand, believe)

positives: I don't remember the title but it's very boring!
I totally understand that you want to go.
negatives: She remembered everything.
They are understanding the lesson.

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple with a limited range of speech act verbs, including 'suggest', 'apologise', 'recommend'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Speech act verbs (suggest, apologise, recommend)

positives: I suggest that you pay for your trip.
I apologise for missing your class.
negatives: She suggested a new plan.
They are recommending this book.

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple with a limited range of reporting verbs, including 'say', 'show'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Reporting verbs (say, show)

positives: Now he says that it improved his social life.
The movie shows how a pretty woman can do different things.
negatives: He said that it was good.
They are showing the movie now.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'yours' after noun + 'of'.

ontology.mental_model: Second-person possession expressed via prepositional phrase.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'of yours' after a noun for emphasis or variation.

positives: You can take a friend of yours.
It was a good idea of yours.
negatives: Your friend is here.
That idea is yours.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronouns 'mine' and 'yours', with singular reference, in comparative clauses after '(not) as … as'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Comparative with mine/yours

positives: My town won't grow as fast as yours.
I need a car as good as mine.
negatives: Your town is bigger than mine.
This lovely bag is yours.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: N/A

positives: This is an impossible match one.
Another impossible match two.
negatives: This is possible.
Another match here.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'yours', with singular reference, in subject position.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possessive pronoun yours as subject

positives: We bought it because yours is very old.
I think yours was very useful.
negatives: This old car is yours.
Your car stopped working.

guideword: FORM: SAME SUBJECT AND OBJECT, SINGULAR
can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of singular reflexive pronouns with an increasing range of verbs to refer to actions where the subject and object of the verb are the same.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using singular reflexives with a variety of verbs as objects

positives: I decided to introduce myself to him.
First you should ask yourself if you have enough money.
negatives: I bought myself a drink.
She went by herself.

can_do_statement: Can use the singular reflexive pronouns 'myself', 'yourself', 'himself' and 'herself' with 'by' to mean alone, without any help.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'by' + singular reflexive pronoun to mean 'alone'

positives: I will study by myself.
He tried to open it by himself.
negatives: I did it myself.
She talked about herself.

can_do_statement: Can use the singular reflexive pronouns 'myself', 'yourself', 'himself' and 'herself' after prepositions where the object of the preposition is the same as the subject of the verb.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using singular reflexives after prepositions

positives: He told me about himself.
She was very proud of herself.
negatives: He opened it by himself.
I enjoyed myself.

can_do_statement: Can use the singular reflexive pronouns 'myself', 'yourself', 'himself' and 'herself' for emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using singular reflexives for emphasis

positives: The director himself guided the actress.
I myself would rather stay at home.
negatives: I cut myself.
He learned it by himself.

can_do_statement: Can use dummy 'it' as a subject to introduce something the speaker or writer is going to refer to.

ontology.mental_model: Dummy 'it' to set up a situation or refer forward
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'it' to introduce a topic

positives: It is best to spend your time in the countryside.
It's normal that your parents want you to go with them.
negatives: It is my favorite book.
It was sitting on the table.

can_do_statement: Can use 'this' as a pronoun to refer back to whole clauses or sentences, especially to highlight or continue an important topic.

ontology.mental_model: Using 'this' to encapsulate a whole preceding proposition.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'This' referring to a whole clause.

positives: He was late, and because of this we missed the train.
You need to stop doing this immediately.
negatives: This apple is very sweet.
I bought this car yesterday.

can_do_statement: Can use 'those' as a pronoun with plural reference.  ►  noun phrases

ontology.mental_model: Using 'those' as a plural demonstrative pronoun.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'Those' as a standalone pronoun.

positives: Those are my favorite shoes!
I want to buy some of those.
negatives: Those people are waiting for you.
I remember those days fondly.

can_do_statement: Can use 'those' as a pronoun to refer to things which have already been mentioned.  ►  noun phrases

ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'Those' referring back.

positives: Those are exactly the things I meant.
I don't like movies like those.
negatives: Those apples look delicious.
Can you pass me those books?

can_do_statement: Can use 'these' as a pronoun with plural reference.  ►  noun phrases

ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'These' as a standalone pronoun.

positives: These are the best cookies I have ever had.
Can you hold these for a second?
negatives: These shoes are too tight.
I don't like these new rules.

can_do_statement: Can use 'these' as a pronoun to refer to something with immediate relevance which has already been mentioned.  ►  noun phrases  ►  pronouns: demonstrative

ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'These' referring back.

positives: These are the reasons I decided to quit.
I have never seen pictures like these.
negatives: These students are very smart.
These days are getting shorter.

can_do_statement: Can use 'this one', 'that one' as a substitute for countable singular nouns that have previously been mentioned.

ontology.mental_model: Lexical substitution using 'one' with a singular demonstrative.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'This one' or 'that one'.

positives: I think I will buy this one.
Could you pass me that one instead?
negatives: This is the only one I have.
That man is the one who helped me.

guideword: FORM: SUBJECT AND OBJECT PRONOUNS, 'BOTH', 'A FEW', 'ANOTHER'
can_do_statement: Can use 'both', 'a few', 'another' as subject and object pronouns.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'both', 'a few', or 'another' without a following noun as standalone pronouns

positives: Both are going to be fine.
Another is ready to go.
negatives: Both cars are fast.
We need another chair.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of pronouns ('some', 'a few', 'any', 'each') with 'of' followed by an object pronoun.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: referring to parts of a specific group using 'some/any/each/a few of'

positives: Some of them are closer.
I like a few of them.
negatives: Some of the people are closer.
Any of the books will do.

can_do_statement: Can use 'this one', 'that one' to refer to a singular countable noun.  ►  pronouns: demonstratives

ontology.mental_model: Demonstrative substitution using 'this one' or 'that one'
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Saying 'this one' or 'that one'

positives: I choose that one, because it is a very good and quiet place.
I'm thinking about buying a new desk because this one is very old.
negatives: This is a dog.
I have that.

can_do_statement: Can use 'one' after 'which' in indirect questions to refer to one of two or more options.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Asking 'which one'

positives: If you ask me which one I would choose, I would first go camping.
This way you see which one is the best.
negatives: Which do you like?
Which of these is better?

can_do_statement: Can use 'ones' as a pronoun to substitute for plural nouns which have already been mentioned or are obvious from the context.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'ones' for plurals

positives: My pillows are getting old and I need new ones.
To tell the truth, I prefer large schools to small ones.
negatives: I have one.
Ones are not numbers.

can_do_statement: Can use premodifiers with 'ones', to refer to something in general.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Adjective + 'ones'

positives: Our computers are out-dated and slow. I think we should replace them with new ones.
Large schools are usually better than small ones.
negatives: I have ones.
The ones we saw were nice.

can_do_statement: Can use determiners + premodifers + 'ones'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using phrases like 'the old ones' or 'some good ones'

positives: I've bought five new t-shirts, because I don't like my old ones anymore.
There are some good ones on the first channel.
negatives: The dog is big.
Some are here.

can_do_statement: Can use 'the ones' with a complement, to refer to something specific.

ontology.mental_model: Specifying specific plural items using 'the ones' with a postmodifier
ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'the ones who/which/that/in/on'

positives: Weddings in our country? Well, they're pretty different from the ones in England.
The products we received were not exactly the ones we ordered.
negatives: The ones are good.
We like the ones.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of indefinite pronouns as objects or complements.

ontology.mental_model: Indefinite entities acting as recipients or descriptors.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using indefinite pronouns as the object of a verb or preposition.

positives: I didn't know anyone at the party.
He saw nothing there.
negatives: Someone was at the door.
Nobody answered the phone.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of indefinite pronouns ('something', 'nobody') as subjects, with a singular verb.

ontology.mental_model: Indefinite entities initiating action or possessing a state.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using indefinite pronouns as subjects taking singular verbs.

positives: Something is happening.
Nobody was there.
negatives: I saw something.
He didn't find anyone.

can_do_statement: Can use 'one' to refer to people in general, in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Generalization of the human subject in a formal register
ontology.pedagogical_hook: formal generic 'one'

positives: The television is a box where one can find anything.
One sees cats everywhere in the city.
negatives: I only have one apple left.
He gave me the red one instead of the blue one.

can_do_statement: Can use premodifiers with indefinite pronouns, often to intensify.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using words like 'absolutely' or 'almost' before indefinite pronouns.

positives: I can find absolutely anything in this store.
Nearly everyone agrees with me.
negatives: I can find anything in this store.
Everyone agrees with me.

can_do_statement: Can use 'each other' as the object of a verb or complement of a preposition to talk about the mutual behaviour of two or more people.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'each other' for mutual interaction

positives: We see each other every day.
They talk to each other.
negatives: Each player has a different role.
They had other ideas.

can_do_statement: Can form alternative question with 'or something else' as the second alternative to a noun phrase, to refer to something non-specific.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'or something else' to broaden options

positives: Shall we buy him a book, a CD or something else?
Do you want to study history, science, or something else?
negatives: I need something else to do.
Or something might happen if we leave.

can_do_statement: Can form alternative questions using 'or not' to substitute for a clause, sometimes to express annoyance or impatience.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'or not' for direct binary alternatives

positives: I asked nervously about his exam, did he pass or not?
Do you agree with me or not?
negatives: Believe it or not, I actually won the race.
Whether you like it or not, we are going.

can_do_statement: Can form alternative questions with two phrases combined with 'or'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Connecting parallel phrases with 'or'

positives: Is this area in the city or in the countryside?
Do you feel more sympathy for your friends or for your parents?
negatives: I like to go in the morning or sleep in.
Is it for me or him?

can_do_statement: Can form alternative questions with two clauses combined with 'or'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Connecting independent clauses with 'or'

positives: Are you still with him or did you two break up?
Should I go there and talk to her or should I stay here?
negatives: Would you like coffee or tea?
Can you bring some food or drinks for the dinner?

guideword: FORM: AFFIRMATIVE MAIN CLAUSES + AFFIRMATIVE QUESTION TAGS
can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of affirmative tags with affirmative clauses.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using affirmative tags for surprise or inference

positives: Your boyfriend is also 16, is he?
You bought new black clothes, did you?
negatives: You didn't buy new clothes, did you?
You are 16, aren't you?

guideword: FORM: AFFIRMATIVE MAIN CLAUSES + NEGATIVE QUESTION TAGS
can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of 'be', 'do', 'have' and modal verb tags with negative main clauses.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using negative tags for expected agreement

positives: And so you're moving to a different area, aren't you?
You'll see the programme on the 23rd of August, won't you?
negatives: You don't like discos, do they?
It isn't a problem, is it?

guideword: FORM: NEGATIVE MAIN CLAUSES + AFFIRMATIVE QUESTION TAGS
can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of affirmative 'be', 'do' and 'have' tags with negative main clauses.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using affirmative tags after negative statements

positives: I mean, your parents don't like discos, do they?
You haven't been to my house before, have you?
negatives: You bought new black clothes, did you?
You love books, don't you?

can_do_statement: Can use 'right' as a tag in informal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'right' for quick confirmation

positives: You are 14 years old, right?
They're black, right?
negatives: Are you sure that's right?
Take a right turn at the next corner.

can_do_statement: Can use 'wh-'words + the negative form of modal verbs + subject + main verb to form 'wh-'questions.

ontology.mental_model: Questioning obstacles or challenging perceived impossibilities
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To challenge or ask about inability/impossibility using negative modals

positives: Why can't you do both things?
How couldn't I control myself?
negatives: I wonder why you can't come.
She asked what I couldn't see.

can_do_statement: Can use main verb 'be' + 'n’t' to form negative 'yes/no' questions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using negative be to ask for confirmation

positives: Isn't it beautiful, man?
Aren't you going to the party?
negatives: It isn't beautiful.
They aren't going to the party.

can_do_statement: Can use auxiliary 'do' and 'have' + 'n’t' + subject + main verb to form negative 'yes/no' questions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using negative auxiliary to ask for confirmation

positives: Don't you agree, friend?
Haven't you finished yet?
negatives: I don't agree.
You haven't seen it.

can_do_statement: Can use modal verbs + 'not' + subject + main verb to form 'yes/no' questions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using negative modal to ask for confirmation

positives: Couldn't you try harder, buddy?
Won't she come with us?
negatives: I couldn't try harder.
She won't come.

can_do_statement: Can use negative 'yes/no' questions to involve the listener or reader by seeking agreement.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using negative questions to seek agreement

positives: It's a great idea, don't you think?
Isn't that amazing?
negatives: I don't think it's a great idea.
I do not think so.

can_do_statement: Can report questions using 'ask' + 'if' or 'whether' + clause, with a pronoun and tense shift where relevant.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using ask if/whether to report yes/no questions

positives: I asked my mom if she wanted to come.
He asks whether it was raining.
negatives: I asked a question.
If she wants to come, ask her.

can_do_statement: Can report speech about events in the future with and without backshifts for words relating to time.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Reporting speech about future events

positives: He says that he would go next week.
She tells me she was leaving tomorrow.
negatives: He went next week.
I will go next week.

can_do_statement: Can report requests and commands with 'ask' or 'tell' + direct object and 'to-'infinitive.

ontology.mental_model: Reported directives mapping a speaker's instruction onto an object via to-infinitive.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Reporting someone else's command or request.

positives: She asked me to come back early.
They told the students to stay in the car.
negatives: I want to ask a question.
He told a story to his friends.

guideword: FORM: DIRECT SPEECH, REPORTING CLAUSE, END POSITION
can_do_statement: Can report speech and thought directly using the reporting verb after the reporting clause.

ontology.mental_model: Direct quotation structured with the reporting clause at the end.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Putting the quoted speech first, then saying who said it.

positives: "I am leaving," she said.
"What is going on?" he asked.
negatives: She said, "I am leaving."
He asked what was going on.

guideword: FORM: DIRECT SPEECH, REPORTING CLAUSE, INITIAL POSITION
can_do_statement: Can report speech and thought directly, using the reporting verb before the reporting clause.

ontology.mental_model: Direct quotation structured with the reporting clause at the beginning.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Saying who spoke before giving their exact words.

positives: She said: "I am going home."
He asked, "Are you coming?"
negatives: "I am going home," she said.
He told me that he was tired.

can_do_statement: Can report thought using 'wonder' + 'wh-'word + clause, with a tense shift where relevant.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing an internal question or uncertainty using 'wonder' followed by a wh-clause.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'wonder' to talk about thoughts and questions.

positives: I wondered what she had written.
He was wondering who the mysterious guest was.
negatives: I wonder if it will rain tomorrow.
It's a wonder how they survived.

can_do_statement: Can use a limited range of verbs + particle + preposition + noun or pronoun.

ontology.mental_model: Spatial action chains mapping abstract state transitions
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Think of the particle and preposition as directions the action takes.

positives: I could catch up with the work I missed after school.
They get on with each other very well.
negatives: I catch a ball when it is thrown.
Look at the big tree.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of prepositional verbs followed by noun or pronoun objects.

ontology.mental_model: Directional verbs leading to target nouns
ontology.pedagogical_hook: These verbs always need their partner preposition to point at the object.

positives: Our company needs to train some staff on how to deal with the complaints.
I completely agree with your proposal.
negatives: We made a great deal today.
I will wait for you outside.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of phrasal verbs + object pronoun + particle.

ontology.mental_model: Manipulating specific, previously mentioned entities with a phrasal verb.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using a pronoun in the middle of a phrasal verb.

positives: I wanted to check it out.
I hate trying them on.
negatives: I wanted to check out the book.
I hate to try on the clothes.

can_do_statement: Can use a limited range of phrasal verbs + particle + object.

ontology.mental_model: Manipulating entities with an inseparable or unseparated phrasal verb.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Keeping the verb and particle together before the object.

positives: I need to pick up my award.
She turned off the phone.
negatives: I picked it up.
She turned it off.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of verbs, typically reporting or mental process verbs, with a 'that'-clause as the direct object.

ontology.mental_model: Formally framing cognitive realisations or statements using explicit subordination
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To explicitly report thoughts or discoveries using verbs followed by a 'that'-clause
ontology.agency_or_distance: Medium agency, structurally distancing the cognitive event from the core statement

positives: I totally understand that you don't want to go.
I realised that I wasn't the only winner.
negatives: I understand your position.
I realised what she was doing.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of phrasal verbs without an object.

ontology.mental_model: Describing intermediate self-contained actions with phrasal verbs.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using intermediate phrasal verbs without an object.

positives: I needed to hang out.
Its battery had run out.
negatives: I will hang it out.
I run the business.

can_do_statement: Can use some reporting verbs with a prepositional phrase followed by a 'that'-clause as the direct object.

ontology.mental_model: Directing a formal report to a specific recipient before declaring the content
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To report statements addressed to specific people using a prepositional phrase before a 'that'-clause
ontology.agency_or_distance: Medium agency, mediating complex information flow to specific listeners

positives: You should say to your parents that you want to try a new experience.
When I said to my friends that I had met with him, they didn't believe me.
negatives: I said that he was coming soon.
He explained the situation to the manager.

guideword: FORM: SEMI-MODAL AUXILIARY VERBS, 'USED TO', 'OUGHT TO'
can_do_statement: Can use semi-modal auxiliary verbs, 'used to' and 'ought to'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using used to and ought to

positives: We used to play together every day.
You ought to join a gym soon.
negatives: I am used to playing with them.
The tool was used to fix the car.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of verbs followed by a 'to-' infinitive.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: verbs (seem, appear, tend, manage) + to infinitive

positives: It seems to be working perfectly.
She managed to finish the race.
negatives: It seems very good.
She promised a big reward.

can_do_statement: Can use a limited range of verbs followed by an '-ing' form.

ontology.mental_model: expanding repertoire of verbs taking gerunds
ontology.pedagogical_hook: verbs (finish, start, mind, keep, suggest) + ing

positives: I finished reading the novel.
Do you mind opening the window?
negatives: I finished the novel.
I started the engine.

can_do_statement: Can use 'make' and 'let' + infinitive without 'to'.

ontology.mental_model: causative and permissive verbs with bare infinitives
ontology.pedagogical_hook: make/let + object + bare infinitive

positives: She always makes me laugh.
They will let us enter early.
negatives: I made it to the party.
Let them be for now.

can_do_statement: Can use 'would prefer' + 'to' infinitive, often for politeness.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: would prefer to + infinitive

positives: I would prefer to stay home tonight.
She'd clearly prefer to work alone.
negatives: I prefer to stay home tonight.
I would prefer a cup of tea.

can_do_statement: Can use 'help' + object + infinitive with or without 'to', with no change in meaning.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: help + object + (to) infinitive

positives: Can you help me find my keys?
It helped them to understand better.
negatives: She is a big help.
I shouted for help loudly.

can_do_statement: Can use some verbs of requesting and commanding followed by a direct object and a 'to-'infinitive.

ontology.mental_model: verbs of commanding and requesting directed at an object
ontology.pedagogical_hook: verbs of requesting/commanding + object + to infinitive

positives: She asked him to leave immediately.
I want you to finish this task.
negatives: She asked to leave immediately.
I want a new computer.

can_do_statement: Can use 'there' with a range of modal verbs + 'be' + complement.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using a modal with 'there' lets you talk about possible or future existence.

positives: There will be flying cars and buses.
In the large school there might be a lot of people.
negatives: There is a flying car outside.
Will there be any people?

can_do_statement: Can use 'There' + 'be' + 'n’t' with countable and uncountable nouns.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Negating the 'be' verb shows something does not exist.

positives: There isn't any noise right now.
There weren't any people on the bus she took.
negatives: They aren't here right now.
We weren't there when it happened.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form with 'I'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: May I

positives: May I ask you a question?
May I help you with that?
negatives: I may go later.
You may ask a question if you want.

can_do_statement: Can use quantifying determiners + 'of' with demonstrative pronouns  ► determiners: demonstrative

ontology.mental_model: Selection from a specific spatial or conceptual set
ontology.pedagogical_hook: quantifier + of + demonstrative

positives: I think you should choose one of these.
We really need to see all of that.
negatives: One of the best things to do is relax.
Some of them are really quite interesting.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of compound adjectives ('up-to-date', 'state-of-the-art')

ontology.mental_model: hyphen as glue for a single complex attribute
ontology.pedagogical_hook: two words, one label

positives: We need to use high-quality materials for the bridge.
She finally found a full-time job.
negatives: I watched Spider-Man yesterday.
It is a very well designed system.

can_do_statement: Can use adjective phrases to modify nouns.

ontology.mental_model: noun narrowed by a participial phrase
ontology.pedagogical_hook: which one? the one built when

positives: I ate a cake completely made of chocolate.
He found a box full of toys.
negatives: The company was making maintenance.
The empty box was there.

can_do_statement: Can use 'slightly' to modify comparative adjectives to a small degree.

ontology.mental_model: slightly nudges one point a hair above the other
ontology.pedagogical_hook: a hair above

negatives: She was slightly tired.
He speaks slightly fast.
positives: The price of a second-hand one was slightly cheaper.
The food of restaurant A is slightly better than that of B.

can_do_statement: Can use 'a lot' to modify and intensify comparative adjectives used predicatively after a verb, usually 'be'.

ontology.mental_model: a lot blows the distance wide open
ontology.pedagogical_hook: blow the gap open

positives: The new design looks a lot better than the old one.
It is a lot cheaper to buy it online.
negatives: Yeah, a lot better.
A lot more people are here.

can_do_statement: Can use 'much' to modify and intensify comparative adjectives used attributively before countable and uncountable nouns.

ontology.mental_model: much + comparative welds a ranked label onto the noun
ontology.pedagogical_hook: rank the noun harder

negatives: It is much better.
I have much more time.
positives: It is a much better investment than the bicycle.
What about a much cheaper hotel like the Plaza?

can_do_statement: Can use 'enough' after adjectives followed by 'to'-infinitive

ontology.mental_model: the threshold reached opens the action
ontology.pedagogical_hook: enough, so it can happen

positives: He is strong enough to lift the heavy box.
She is old enough to drive a car.
negatives: I feel like I'm not good enough to Yeah.
I do not have big enough for this.

can_do_statement: Can form adjective phrases with 'rather a' + adjective, often in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: rather a marks measured, formal assessment
ontology.pedagogical_hook: formal understatement

negatives: I would rather stay at home.
It is rather cold outside.
positives: Films tend to be rather a simple art.
I must confess that I'm rather a poor player.

can_do_statement: Can use the adjectives 'present', 'future', 'former' before a noun.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: present / future / former + noun — mark an entity with its temporal qualifier attributively
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker slots an entity into its temporal slot

positives: I am quite happy with my present situation.
He is the former president of the company.
negatives: In the future, we will have flying cars.
I will present the results to the boss.

can_do_statement: Can use a limited range of degree adjectives ('real', 'absolute', 'complete') before a noun to express intensity.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: real / absolute / complete + noun — name the entity at the upper extreme of its scale
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker escalates the noun to its extreme

positives: The party was a complete disaster from start to finish.
I think he is an absolute beginner.
negatives: I have to complete all the tasks today.
This is a big problem in real life.

can_do_statement: Can use the premodifer 'by far' to make a superlative adjective stronger.

ontology.mental_model: Amplifying the certainty and degree of a superlative claim
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'by far' to strongly emphasize a superlative

positives: This one is by far the most beautiful of all.
Christmas morning was by far the most exciting and happiest moment.
negatives: It is the most beautiful.
He went by far too quickly.

can_do_statement: Can use '(one of) the' with an increasing range of superlative adjectives without a following noun, when the noun is understood.

ontology.mental_model: Identifying one of the extreme points on a scale without explicitly naming the entity
ontology.pedagogical_hook: When describing extremes, say 'one of the best' and stop there if the noun is obvious.

positives: It's very difficult to pick the most embarrassing.
That period of my life was one of the worst .
negatives: It was one of the worst moments of my life.
He is the greatest player in the team.

can_do_statement: Can use superlative adjectives before a noun + 'to'-infinitive. ► clauses: comparative

ontology.mental_model: Prescribing the optimal action or entity for a purpose
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Combining superlatives with infinitives to give strong recommendations

positives: The easiest way to do it is to use computers.
A bicycle is perhaps the cheapest way to travel in the city.
negatives: It is the easiest way.
He wants the best to win.

sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of manner adverbs to modify how something happpens.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: seriously / completely / entirely / carefully / properly — wider texture palette for HOW
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker expands the texture vocabulary of the action

positives: She handled the fragile glass very carefully.
The snow melted gradually over the week.
negatives: Well, there are other topics we can discuss.
I am fully of work right now.

sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of adverbs and adverb phrases to refer to the timing of an event.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: shortly / immediately / eventually / finally / currently / nowadays — finer temporal pointers
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker pins the event on a granular S-anchored line

positives: We will shortly arrive at the main station.
I have recently finished reading that book.
negatives: Today I do not have the internet in my office.
Tomorrow I will have a lot of news.

can_do_statement: Can use degree adverbs ('almost', 'very') to modify determiners. ► determiners

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'almost' or 'very' right before quantity words like 'all' or 'few'.

positives: I can work at home almost all the time.
There are probably very few of us.
negatives: It is almost ready.
She is very happy.

can_do_statement: Can use degree adverbs to modify pronouns. ► pronouns

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using degree to modify completeness of sets

positives: You can buy absolutely anything you like.
She said almost nothing during the meeting.
negatives: The dog is absolutely adorable.
Almost all the people left early.

can_do_statement: Can use degree adverbs to modify noun phrases. ► noun phrases

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Adverbs adjusting nominal precision

positives: It would be quite a formal meeting.
After all, he is almost a human.
negatives: I was quite tired.
She rather enjoys walking.

can_do_statement: Can use 'never' in front position followed by an inverted subject (most commonly 'I') + main verb verb, to give focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Never + aux + I/you/we/they + verb — flip the clause around 'never' for dramatic focus
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker front-loads 'never' and rearranges the clause for emphasis

positives: Never have I seen such a realistic and impressive film before.
Never had I thought that would happen.
negatives: I never have seen such a realistic film.
I never go there.

can_do_statement: Can modify an adverb with a comparative structure.

ontology.mental_model: Comparing the manner or frequency of actions dynamically
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using comparative structures to modify adverbs

positives: Profits will rise even more sharply than last year.
We can search information much more quickly than before.
negatives: He is much more interesting.
It is even more beautiful.

can_do_statement: Can use 'the same' (+ noun) + 'as' + clause.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Equating current reality with past facts

positives: Maybe I'll do the same thing as you did.
Some people say that friendship today is not the same as it used to be.
negatives: We wear the same uniform as you.
I bought the same book as my brother.

can_do_statement: Can use 'enough' after adjectives followed by 'to'-infinitive.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Reaching a threshold for capability

positives: Young people are not mature enough to decide by themselves.
I think I am responsible enough to handle this job.
negatives: We have enough food to eat.
I didn't sleep enough to feel rested.

can_do_statement: Can use a superlative adjective (+ noun) (+ 'that') followed by a clause to talk about something unique.

ontology.mental_model: Identifying unique or extreme instances within a category.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Superlative highlighting with relative clauses.

positives: In my opinion this is the worst thing that can ever happen.
That is the clearest thing I can remember.
negatives: He is the tallest boy in the class.
She did the best.

can_do_statement: .||Can use than + an increasing range of non-finite clauses (to-infinitive, reduced clause)  forming the second part of a comparison after a comparative adjective||

ontology.mental_model: Comparing an entity's quality against an action or state.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Comparative adjective followed by a non-finite clause.

positives: It is much easier to be single than to have a partner.
I think that arbitration is more appropriate than to file an action in court against the tenant.
negatives: He is taller than his brother.
I like tea more than coffee.

can_do_statement: Can use 'rather than' + a non-finite clause to stress one element in a comparison.

ontology.mental_model: Selecting one option over another with explicit contrast.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'rather than' with non-finite clauses.

positives: If you prefer watching TV rather than reading, you have to be critical.
I would prefer to sleep in tents rather than stay in rooms.
negatives: I would rather go home.
I like cats rather than dogs.

guideword: FORM: 'AS IF' OR 'AS THOUGH' + FINITE CLAUSE
can_do_statement: Can use 'as if' or 'as though' + finite clause to introduce a second clause as a comparison.

ontology.mental_model: Projecting a hypothetical situation as a point of comparison.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'as if' or 'as though' with finite clauses.

positives: Her heart beat extremely fast, as if it was going to burst out of her chest.
Everything was so familiar, so close, as though he had never left the place.
negatives: She acts as if to speak.
It looks as if trying to run.

can_do_statement: Can combine two main clauses of the same type using 'neither' in front or mid position, followed by 'nor' to introduce the second clause, for emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Saying 'not this and not that'

positives: They neither got married nor had children.
We neither walk nor do exercises.
negatives: I want neither of them.
Nor did I know about it.

can_do_statement: Can combine clauses using 'not only' in mid position of the first clause followed by … 'but (also)' to introduce the second clause, to give focus.

ontology.mental_model: Adding emphasis to a second point
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasizing two related points

positives: It is nice not only because it is colorful, but because I like it.
He not only studies hard, but also plays well.
negatives: Not only was he there, but she was too.
This is my only hope.

can_do_statement: Can use 'let's not' + base form of a main verb to make a suggestion.

positives: Let's not lose track of each other again!
Let's not make the situation more complicated.
negatives: Let's go home now.
He let us not participate in the race.

can_do_statement: Can use 'do not' for emphasis or in formal contexts.

positives: Do not hesitate to contact me.
Do not forget your passport.
negatives: We do not accept cash.
I do not understand.

can_do_statement: Can form negative interrogative clauses with an adverb in mid position, between the subject and the main verb.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Negative questions with adverbs

positives: Why don't you ever listen to me?
Haven't you ever heard about the photographer?
negatives: Don't you listen to me?
Why do you always listen to me?

can_do_statement: Can use the negative interrogative form of an auxiliary verb to express surprise or enthusiasm.

ontology.mental_model: Using a negative question format to express positive enthusiasm or surprise.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Exclamatory use of negative interrogative.

positives: Wouldn't it be wonderful!
Doesn't that sound excellent to you?!
negatives: He isn't here.
Isn't it a wonderful day?

can_do_statement: Can use defining relative clauses and non-defining relative clauses ending in a preposition, with 'who/which/that' as the complement of the preposition.

ontology.mental_model: Connecting a relative pronoun to its required preposition
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Ending a relative clause with a preposition when the pronoun is the complement
ontology.agency_or_distance: Syntactic deferral by moving the preposition to the end of the clause

positives: They have three children who I love to play with.
It was a case that he had nothing to do with!
negatives: I know the man who is with her.
The book which is on the table is mine.

can_do_statement: Can use non-defining relative clauses with 'whose', to give additional information.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using a non-defining relative clause with 'whose' to add extra details about what someone owns or their relationships
ontology.agency_or_distance: Distance from core identity by adding supplementary possessive description

positives: I met a friend, whose job is to organise shows.
I have an assistant, whose parents are nice.
negatives: The man whose car was stolen was sad.
I wonder whose this is.

can_do_statement: Can use defining relative clauses with 'whose', to give more information about relationship.

ontology.mental_model: Defining a person by their relationships or possessions
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'whose' in a defining relative clause to specify exactly who is being discussed based on relation
ontology.agency_or_distance: Anchoring identity to an external, possessed relational entity

positives: I teach children whose parents immigrated here.
Mary is a lady whose parents died.
negatives: My friend, whose job is great, is rich.
I wonder whose coat this is.

can_do_statement: Can use a relative clause to refer to a whole clause or sentence, often to express an opinion or evaluation or give a reason.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'which' referring back to a whole clause to give an opinion or evaluation
ontology.agency_or_distance: Metalinguistic distance in commenting on a complete thought

positives: He passed the exam, which is great.
It was raining, which meant we stayed inside.
negatives: The book, which I read, is mine.
I bought a car which is very fast.

can_do_statement: Can use a non-finite subordinate clause with 'after' + 'having/being' + '-ed' form, before a main clause, to refer to past time.

ontology.mental_model: Sequencing past events with perfect participle
ontology.pedagogical_hook: After having done...

positives: After having worked for many hours, you'll be tired.
After being given the pass, you can take pictures.
negatives: After working all day, I went home.
He arrived after having a big dinner.

can_do_statement: Can use a finite subordinate clause, before or after a main clause, with conjunctions to introduce conditions. ► clauses: conditionals

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Conditionals with unless/provided

positives: Unless something is done, many people will die.
Provided the weather is fine, you could go swimming.
negatives: I was provided with a new laptop for work.
He provided that information yesterday.

can_do_statement: Can use a non-finite clause, introduced by '-ing' before a main clause, to give more information.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Fronted -ing clauses

positives: Having no choice, I sat down on a bench.
Using his best smile, Paul asked her.
negatives: Running is good for you.
Swimming makes me hungry.

can_do_statement: Can use conditional subordinate clauses with a range of conjunctions ('as long as', 'provided') + present simple or present continuous, with future reference.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'as long as' or 'provided' to set conditions.

positives: As long as it involves children I'd be delighted.
We offer a discount provided you reserve space.
negatives: It is as long as a car.
They provided us with food.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'BOTH … AND' WITH PHRASES AND CLAUSES
can_do_statement: Can use 'both … and' to combine phrases and clauses, often for emphasis.

ontology.mental_model: Emphasizing the inclusion of two distinct structural components (phrases/clauses).
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Apply 'both...and' not just to single words, but to whole phrases for stronger emphasis.

positives: They succeeded both at home and abroad.
The device can both entertain users and educate them.
negatives: Both the cat and dog slept.
I like them both.

can_do_statement: Can use 'neither … nor' to connect two words, phrases or clauses, often to give emphasis or focus.

ontology.mental_model: Emphasizing the exclusion of two alternatives.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'neither...nor' to strongly state that not one, and not the other, is true.

positives: Neither John nor Mary knew the answer.
We can neither eat nor drink in the library.
negatives: Neither of us wanted to go.
I don't know, nor do I care.

can_do_statement: Can use more complex subordinating conjunctions ('as long as, as soon as, in order that, despite the fact that, due to the fact that, as if, as though') to introduce a subordinate clause.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: complex subordinating conjunctions

positives: I decided to go to Paris as soon as I finished university.
Everything was so familiar, as though he had never left the place.
negatives: I have as many as you.
It is due to the weather.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of simple subordinating conjunctions ('once, whereas, unless, except (that) provided (that)'), to introduce a subordinate clause.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: conditional and concessive subordinators

positives: Once you become an employee, you'll get discounts.
I can't say that I've changed much, except that now I'm blond!
negatives: I did it once.
Everyone came except John.

can_do_statement: Can use the in comparative phrases 'more', 'less', 'worse', 'better … the more', 'less', 'worse …' to talk about one thing that is affected by another. ► comparative clauses

ontology.mental_model: Correlative comparatives showing parallel increase or decrease.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'The more... the more...' structure shows a direct relationship between two changes.

positives: The more you watch, the worse you become.
The better education you have, the better opportunities you get.
negatives: I want the more expensive one.
It is getting worse and worse.

can_do_statement: Can use ''s' after a noun phrase with of to indicate possession.

ontology.mental_model: Mapping possession, quantification, or specific reference to an entity.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Identifying the scope or owner of a noun phrase.

positives: He is a friend of my father's.
I heard a story of your brother's.
negatives: He is a friend of my father.
My father's friend is here.

can_do_statement: Can use 's'' after plural nouns to indicate possession.

ontology.mental_model: Mapping possession, quantification, or specific reference to an entity.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Identifying the scope or owner of a noun phrase.

positives: We stayed at my parents' house.
I want to study animals' behaviour.
negatives: The cat's toy is missing.
It's a beautiful day.

can_do_statement: Can use 'their' before nouns to refer to a generic body or group of people expressed as a singular subject. ► generic pronouns

ontology.mental_model: Mapping possession, quantification, or specific reference to an entity.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Identifying the scope or owner of a noun phrase.

positives: Everyone has their own opinion.
Every customer wants their product fast.
negatives: Their car is parked outside.
Everyone knows he is right.

can_do_statement: Can use possessive determiner 'its' before nouns to refer to a singular inanimate subject or object.

ontology.mental_model: Mapping possession, quantification, or specific reference to an entity.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Identifying the scope or owner of a noun phrase.

positives: It has its own screen.
Verona is great with its buildings.
negatives: It's a huge screen.
I love its.

can_do_statement: Can use modifier + 'little' + uncountable nouns and modifier + 'few' + countable nouns, to indicate a lack of something or not as much as expected of something.► adverbs

ontology.mental_model: Emphasizing a scarcity or lack of quantity using modifiers.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'very little' or 'so few'.

positives: I spend very little time outside.
There are so few animals living there.
negatives: I have a little time left.
A few friends came over.

can_do_statement: Can use a range of phrases as discourse markers to introduce a comparison.

ontology.mental_model: Drawing parallels between two states or events.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'likewise' or 'similarly'.

positives: Likewise, in Nepal New Year is celebrated on 1st of Baishak.
Similarly, the population of children are likely to drop.
negatives: They walk identically.
He is very similar to me.

can_do_statement: Can use a range of phrases as discourse markers to summarise.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'thus', 'consequently', 'therefore'.

positives: Thus, I would be very grateful.
Consequently, visiting zoos can help people.
negatives: They lived happily ever after.
So I went to the store.

guideword: FORM/USE: ORGANISING, OPENINGS AND CLOSINGS, FORMAL
can_do_statement: Can use a range of phrases as discourse markers to open and close texts and point to conclusions, often in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Formal sectioning of arguments

positives: In conclusion, the experiment was a complete success.
In summary, we need to focus on cost reduction.
negatives: We arrived at the same conclusion yesterday.
He gave a quick summary of the plot.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'THE THING/ FACT/ POINT/ PROBLEM IS (THAT)'
can_do_statement: Can use 'The thing, fact, point, problem, or reason + is (that)' for focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Drawing attention to the main point

positives: The problem is that we don't have enough time.
The point is, we need to try harder.
negatives: I completely understand the problem.
That is a very interesting fact.

can_do_statement: Can use 'The reason (that)', 'The place (which)' + clause as subject + 'be' for focus. ► Relative clauses

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Defining the specific reason or place

positives: The reason I called is to ask for your help.
The place we visited was absolutely stunning.
negatives: I do not know the reason for his departure.
This is the place where we met.

can_do_statement: Can use the future continuous with 'will' as a polite question form, in place of the present simple or future simple.

ontology.mental_model: Softening a question by shifting it into a progressive future aspect
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'Will I be -ing?' to ask questions more politely.

positives: Will I be needing any money?
Will you be requiring further assistance today?
negatives: Will they be needing any help?
I will be needing some money.

can_do_statement: Can use 'yes/no' and 'wh-' question forms with 'will'.

ontology.mental_model: Inquiring about an ongoing action in the future
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'Will... be -ing?' to ask about future plans in progress.

positives: Will they be holding any activities at night?
What will you be doing in a few years from now?
negatives: They will be holding activities at night.
Will you do that for me?

can_do_statement: Can use the present forms of 'be' + 'about to'.

ontology.mental_model: Positioning an event on the immediate verge of occurrence
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'am/is/are about to' when something is going to happen very soon.

positives: You are not going to believe what I am about to tell you!
I'm in a hurry, my class is about to begin.
negatives: I was about to begin when the phone rang.
They were about to win the game.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be due to' and, more formally, 'be to' talk about things that are scheduled or expected.

ontology.mental_model: Framing an action as formally scheduled
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'be due to' or 'be to' for scheduled future events.

positives: Our annual conference is due to take place next week.
We are to leave a bit earlier today.
negatives: I was due to go yesterday.
I have to leave right now.

can_do_statement: Can use the present form of 'be' + 'to'.

ontology.mental_model: Framing an action as formally scheduled or required
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'is to' or 'are to' for formal arrangements.

positives: I am to go on a business trip to New York.
He is to come to Athens next Friday.
negatives: I have to go to work.
I am planning to come.

guideword: USE: OBLIGATIONS AND  INSTRUCTIONS WITH 'BE TO'
can_do_statement: Can use 'be to' talk about future obligations and to give instructions.

ontology.mental_model: Imposing an obligation using a formal construction
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'you are to' to give strict instructions.

positives: You're to sit in front of the TV.
They are to have their passports ready.
negatives: They are sitting in front of the TV.
You have to sit here.

guideword: USE: IMMEDIATE FUTURE WITH 'BE ABOUT TO'
can_do_statement: Can use 'be about to' to talk about the immediate future, often with 'just'.

ontology.mental_model: Positioning an event on the immediate verge of occurrence with emphasis
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'just about to' for things happening right this second.

positives: We are just about to launch a new product.
I'm just about to call him.
negatives: We are about to launch a product.
I am just calling him now.

can_do_statement: Can use the present form of 'be' + 'due to'.

ontology.mental_model: Framing an action as formally scheduled using 'due to'
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'is due to' for scheduled events.

positives: I am due to start work in August.
We are due to be present at the meeting.
negatives: I was due to start work last week.
The assignment is due tomorrow.

ontology.mental_model: ongoing action incomplete at a future point
ontology.pedagogical_hook: expressing that an action will not have been continuing up to a future point

positives: I will not have been working here for long.
They won't have been studying for three hours.
negatives: I will not have finished my homework by then.
He hasn't been working here long.

can_do_statement: Can use the affirmative form with 'will'.

ontology.mental_model: ongoing action completed at a future point
ontology.pedagogical_hook: emphasising duration of an activity looking back from a future point

positives: This summer I will have been working for three years.
By then, she'll have been studying for an hour.
negatives: I will have been to London.
I will not have been working here for long.

can_do_statement: Can use the simple past form of 'be' + 'on the point of' + '-ing' to talk about things that were expected to happen soon after a point in the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: emphasizing an action that was very close to happening

positives: I was on the point of leaving the office.
They were on the point of catching him.
negatives: I am on the point of leaving.
He made a point of talking to everyone.

can_do_statement: Can use the simple past form of 'be' + 'about to' (often with 'just') to talk about the immediate future from a point in the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: expressing that something was just going to happen

positives: I was just about to write you a letter.
Our father was about to buy a brand new car.
negatives: I am about to leave.
It was about a boy who went to space.

guideword: USE: LOOKING BACK FROM A POINT IN THE FUTURE
can_do_statement: Can use the future perfect continuous to look back to the past from a point in the future and to emphasise the duration of an activity or event.

ontology.mental_model: duration of an activity looking back from the future
ontology.pedagogical_hook: emphasising how long something will have been going on by a certain future time

positives: This month, I will have been studying English for seven months.
I will have been working for my company for one year by the end of June.
negatives: I imagine you will have been waiting outside.
I won't have been studying.

can_do_statement: Can use the affirmative form with 'will'.

ontology.mental_model: event completed before a future time
ontology.pedagogical_hook: expressing that something will be finished before a point in the future

positives: I'm sure I will have learned today's lesson by the next lesson.
The role of clothes will have disappeared by the year 2050.
negatives: I will have been learning English for ten years.
I won't have finished my work by then.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form with 'will'.

ontology.mental_model: event not completed before a future time
ontology.pedagogical_hook: expressing that something will not be finished before a point in the future

positives: I will not have finished my university exams by June.
We won't have done more than 40 km.
negatives: I will have learned the lesson by then.
They haven't done it yet.

guideword: USE: EVENTS COMPLETED IN THE FUTURE
can_do_statement: Can use the future perfect simple with 'will' to talk about something which is expected to be completed (or not completed) by a certain point in the future.

ontology.mental_model: event completed before a future time
ontology.pedagogical_hook: expressing that something will be finished before a point in the future

positives: The match will have finished by that time.
You will have saved more money at the end of the month.
negatives: I will have finished the book.
I will not have been working here for long.

can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous with a wide range of verbs to talk about future arrangements.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: present continuous for arrangements (B2)

positives: We're throwing a party for fun on 5th January.
She is joining the course on Friday.
negatives: We threw a party last week.
Are you joining the course?

can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous with a wide range of common verbs to ask about future plans.

ontology.mental_model: inquiry about fixed arrangement in the future
ontology.pedagogical_hook: present continuous for future questions (B2)

positives: So are you planning to visit Japan then?
When is the festival starting?
negatives: Do you provide seminar materials?
I am planning to visit Japan.

can_do_statement: Can use 'it' + linking verb + adjective + ('that') clause.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Presenting facts or possibilities objectively

positives: It seems clear to me that swimming is good.
It is obvious that some people prefer reading.
negatives: The answer seems clear.
His mistake is obvious to everyone.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'IT' + LINKING VERB + ADJECTIVES + CLAUSE, HEDGING
can_do_statement: Can use 'it' + linking verb + adjective + ('that') clause to make an assertion less direct.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Softening claims to avoid absolute certainty

positives: It does not seem possible that we can live without it.
It is likely that we will learn some new words.
negatives: The plan seems possible.
It is clear that he is right.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'IT' + LINKING VERB + ADJECTIVES + ('THAT') CLAUSE, FOCUS
can_do_statement: Can use 'it' + linking verb + adjective + ('that') clause as a focusing device.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Highlighting a key fact or necessity

positives: It is clear that we can't live without computers.
It seems obvious that this oil comes from there.
negatives: The message is clear.
It is possible that it rains.

can_do_statement: Can use pronoun or noun + 'be' + adjective + 'to' + (past) infinitive.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Expressing likelihood about someone or something

positives: They are unlikely to arrive on Friday.
We are sure to increase our turnover.
negatives: It is unlikely that they will arrive.
Are you sure about this?

can_do_statement: Can use 'can' with an increasing range of adverbs (including 'easily', 'hardly', 'now', 'probably', 'sometimes', 'still') in the normal mid position after the modal verb or after the subject in questions.  ► adverbs

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using specific adverbs like easily, hardly, probably with 'can'

positives: I can easily provide references for you.
You can hardly imagine how tired I am.
negatives: I can do it easily if you want.
She hardly can do anything right.

can_do_statement: Can use 'can' to talk about general truths and tendencies.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'can' to express tendencies

positives: Too much work can cause stress.
Young people can feel bored at museums.
negatives: I can feel the wind.
He can make a cake.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative forms of 'can't' and 'cannot' to guess, predict and deduce.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'can't be' for deductions

positives: It can't be true what they are saying.
You cannot be feeling well if you look so pale.
negatives: I can't swim.
We cannot park here.

can_do_statement: Can use negative forms of 'can' to make reproaches or appeals.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'can't' to appeal to someone's reason

positives: You can't forget your friends like that.
Can't you see how exhausted you are?
negatives: I can't see anything without my glasses.
We can't forget the date.

can_do_statement: Can use negative form dare not and daren't +  infinitive without to.

ontology.mental_model: Agent expresses an internal barrier or lack of courage preventing an action using 'dare not' or 'daren't'.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Lacking the courage to act
ontology.agency_or_distance: Agency: grappling with internal fears or boundaries

positives: But many local people dare not go to Lily, because it is too expensive.
they daren't give up their car.
negatives: I dare say you are right.
I didn't dare to move.

can_do_statement: Can use affirmative form dare + infinitive without to.

ontology.mental_model: Agent asserts courage or challenges boundaries by acting, using 'dare' + bare infinitive.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Having the bravery to act
ontology.agency_or_distance: Agency: asserting volition and overcoming fear

positives: I can cook if you dare eat it!
I wonder if he dare jump.
negatives: How dare you speak to me like that!
I dare say you are right.

can_do_statement: Can use semi-modal 'dare' to talk about being brave enough to do something.

ontology.mental_model: Agent uses 'dare' as a semi-modal to discuss the internal threshold of courage required for an action.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Discussing bravery and nerve
ontology.agency_or_distance: Agency: evaluating the fortitude to cross a boundary

positives: I think that they are rather jealous because they daren't give up their car.
She dare not tell him the truth.
negatives: I dare say it will rain.
I double dare you to do it.

can_do_statement: Can use the full range of expressions with 'be' + infinitive ('be likely to', 'be due to', 'be meant to', 'be bound to', 'be sure to', 'be certain to', 'be obliged to') with present and past forms of 'be' and with modal 'will' .
