ontology.mental_model: Degrees of certainty, expectation, and obligation
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Advanced phrases with 'be'

positives: We are bound to make mistakes.
She is certain to win the competition.
negatives: I am supposed to leave now.
He was able to finish the puzzle.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be meant to' to talk about ideal states.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Expressing how things should naturally be

positives: We are meant to learn from our mistakes.
It is meant to be a relaxing vacation.
negatives: I meant to call you earlier.
She was bound to find out the truth.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be due to' and, more formally, 'be to' to talk about things that are scheduled or expected.

ontology.mental_model: Future plans based on fixed schedules
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Formal scheduling

positives: The train is due to arrive at noon.
I am to start my new job on Monday.
negatives: I am going to the store.
It is due to the bad weather.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be' (+modifier) 'likely to' to talk about probability.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Predicting likely events

positives: It is very likely to rain this evening.
They are likely to forget the appointment.
negatives: I like to play basketball.
She is more likely to succeed.

can_do_statement: Can use '(much) more/less' to modify 'likely' in a comparison.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Comparing likelihoods

positives: You are much less likely to get sick if you wash your hands.
Older cars are more likely to break down.
negatives: She is likely to arrive on time.
I liked the movie more than the book.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be supposed to' to talk about hearsay or supposition.

ontology.mental_model: Information received through rumor or popular belief
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Reporting what people say

positives: The new restaurant is supposed to be amazing.
He is supposed to have won the lottery.
negatives: I am supposed to finish my homework.
They supposed that he was right.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be' (+ modifier) 'bound to' to talk about something certain or inevitable.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be bound to

positives: It is bound to happen sooner or later.
They're almost bound to find out.
negatives: The package is bound for London.
He bound the pages to the cover.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be' + 'obvious/sure/likely/certain' followed by a 'that'-clause.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be obvious/sure/likely/certain that

positives: It is obvious that he lied.
I am quite sure that they will win.
negatives: Are you sure of that?
That is a likely story.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be supposed to' to talk about expectation or obligation.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be supposed to

positives: We are supposed to leave now.
I am not supposed to be here.
negatives: I supposed to myself that he was right.
The supposed rules were unclear.

can_do_statement: Can use the imperative form 'be sure to', to express obligation.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: imperative be sure to

positives: Be sure to contact me.
Please be sure to tell him.
negatives: I want to be sure to get there.
Are you sure to go?

can_do_statement: Can use 'be sure to', 'be certain to' to talk about certainty.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be sure/certain to

positives: You are sure to find it.
They're almost certain to win.
negatives: I am sure of that.
Be sure to do it.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be forced to' to talk about an unnamed obligation, where the circumstances are beyond the control of the speaker/writer.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be forced to

positives: I was forced to leave.
We are forced to cut the budget.
negatives: He forced me to go.
The forced labor was hard.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be obliged to' to talk about an external obligation, especially in institutional contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be obliged to

positives: We are obliged to wear a uniform.
They were obliged to give up their house.
negatives: I felt obliged to him.
He obliged me to do it.

can_do_statement: Can use 'you (have) got to' to make a strong suggestion.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: you have got to for advice

positives: You've got to see this movie.
You have to try the pie here.
negatives: I have got to leave now.
You have to be kidding me.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may' with an increasing range of adverbs (most commonly 'even', 'only', 'already', 'never', 'just', 'sometimes') in the normal mid-position after the modal verb. ► adverbs

ontology.pedagogical_hook: may even/never/just

positives: You may even find it useful.
They may never know the truth.
negatives: I may go there sometimes.
May I just say something?

can_do_statement: Can use 'may I' to make a polite request, command or suggestion in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: May I for formal request

positives: May I have your attention please?
May I suggest a different approach?
negatives: May I go to the bathroom?
I may have a suggestion.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may have' + '-ed' to talk about possibility in the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: When you guess about what happened before now, use 'may have' plus the past participle.

positives: He may have forgiven me for that accident.
As you may have noticed, there has been a delay.
negatives: He may have a new car.
May we have some water?

can_do_statement: Can use 'may I' to make a polite request for permission.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To ask for permission in a formal or polite way, start with 'May I'.

positives: Sir, may I come in?
May I ask you if your special offer will be still available?
negatives: He may go to the store.
The month of May is warm.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may' in phrases such as as 'you may know', or 'as you may have' + '-ed' to focus the reader on shared knowledge.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To remind someone of something they probably know, use 'as you may know' or 'as you may have heard'.

positives: As you may know, it takes many hours.
As you may have heard, I am going to change to the engineering department.
negatives: You may leave when you are ready.
He may know the answer to the question.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may … but' to express an unexpected point of view.

ontology.mental_model: Conceding a point before introducing a counter-argument
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To agree with something briefly before adding a surprising twist, use 'may' followed by 'but'.

positives: This may surprise you but I've managed to lose some weight.
You may think that it is quite boring but it is not.
negatives: He may go to the store, but I don't think he will.
May I go? But why?

can_do_statement: Can use the question form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Asking about obligations

positives: Must I cancel my trip to India?
How much money must we bring with us?
negatives: You must cancel your trip to India.
I must bring my own money with me.

can_do_statement: Can use 'must have' + '-ed'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Speculating on the past

positives: When I realized that he must have forgotten, I called him up.
I must have fallen about fifty times.
negatives: You must have a ticket to enter.
I must have it by tomorrow.

can_do_statement: Can use the fixed expression 'I must say' to give emphasis, usually about something positive.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Giving emphasis

positives: I must say that I'm most delighted to have you here with us.
I must say they were absolutely superb.
negatives: You must say what you think.
He must say sorry to her.

can_do_statement: Can use 'must' with an increasing range of adverbs (including 'all', 'never', 'strongly', 'first') in the normal mid position after the modal verb. ► adverbs

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasizing rules or duties

positives: We must all act immediately because humanity may be in danger.
There is one thing we must never forget.
negatives: All the students must wait outside.
You never must speak to me like that.

can_do_statement: Can use 'must' to ask about obligation and necessity.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Asking about obligations

positives: Must I cancel my trip to India?
How much money must we bring with us?
negatives: You must cancel your trip to India.
I must bring my own money with me.

can_do_statement: Can use the perfect form of 'must' to make deductions about the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Speculating on past states

positives: Of course, India must have changed a lot since then.
I must have clearly looked awful that day.
negatives: You must have a license to drive.
He must have the right tools for the job.

can_do_statement: Can use the fixed expression 'I must admit' or 'you must admit' to express concession.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Acknowledging points

positives: On the other hand you must admit that they taste good.
I must admit that I completely agree with Chris.
negatives: He must admit his mistake immediately.
They must admit that they were wrong.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative forms of 'must' to talk about what is not permitted.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Establishing rules

positives: You must not hit them or punish them without good reason.
You mustn't talk during lessons.
negatives: I must not only run but also jump.
The must knot on the boat broke.

can_do_statement: Can use 'ought to' without a following verb where the previous main verb is understood. ► ellipsis

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Ending a clause with 'ought to'

positives: They did not get as much help as they ought to.
She isn't practicing as much as she really ought to!
negatives: She ought to practice more.
They ought to go home.

can_do_statement: Can use 'needn't to' talk about a lack of obligation.

ontology.mental_model: Absence of current or general necessity
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'needn't' followed by a base verb

positives: We needn't wear a jacket today.
You needn't worry about the music.
negatives: We don't need to wear a jacket.
You needn't have worried.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form.

ontology.mental_model: Negative modality expressing lack of obligation
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Forming the negative without auxiliary 'do'

positives: You need not actually worry about the time.
She needn't go out jogging tonight.
negatives: She doesn't need to go out.
They did not need it.

can_do_statement: Can use 'ought to' to talk about desired states of affairs.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing how things ideally should be
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'ought to' for broad ideals and states

positives: Not all zoos are as good as they ought to be.
Furthermore, we ought to take care of our health.
negatives: There ought to be more excursions.
They ought to have gone home.

can_do_statement: Can use 'should' and 'shouldn't' without a following verb where the previous main verb is understood.

ontology.mental_model: Omitting the main verb when it is already known from context.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Agree with a suggestion without repeating it: 'I think you should.'

positives: Well, have you ever checked your blood pressure? I think you should.
he wanted to answer and meet her again, but he knew that he shouldn't.
negatives: You should bring your guitar.
You shouldn't have done that.

can_do_statement: Can use 'should be' + '-ing'.

ontology.mental_model: A continuous action is recommended or expected right now.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: What is someone supposed to be doing right now? Say 'They should be working'.

positives: Well, you should be bouncing up and down with joy!
We should be reading books instead of watching television.
negatives: It should be a good day.
We should read books instead of watching television.

can_do_statement: Can use 'should be' + '-ing' to talk about present general obligation.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing a continuous duty or rule that applies generally.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: What is the rule? Say 'Animals should be running free'.

positives: Wild animals should be running free.
If a driver has drunk alcohol, he shouldn't be driving.
negatives: You should be bouncing up and down with joy!
The computer systems should be working again.

can_do_statement: Can use 'should be' + '-ing' to talk about expectations.

ontology.mental_model: Predicting a continuous state based on a plan or typical behavior.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: What's expected to happen? Say 'The situation should be improving'.

positives: The computer systems should be working again once you restart them.
The situation should be improving in the next 6 months.
negatives: We should be reading books.
Wild animals should be running free.

can_do_statement: Can use 'used to' without a following verb where the previous main verb is understood. ► ellipsis

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Ending sentences with used to

positives: She doesn't travel as much as she used to.
They sound quite a lot better than they used to!
negatives: I used to travel a lot.
He used to be my friend.

can_do_statement: Can use 'will' (particularly 'Will you please') to make requests and commands in a wide range of contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'will you' to firmly request or command

positives: Will you please send me his name?
Will you pay attention to the screen!
negatives: When will you arrive?
I think you will do it nicely.

can_do_statement: Can use 'would' to talk about habitual actions and events in the past.

ontology.mental_model: Describing repeated actions in the past.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'would' for habitual past actions.

positives: As a child, I would always play outside.
We would often go to the beach.
negatives: I would like to play outside.
She said she would go tomorrow.

can_do_statement: Can used 'could' have + '-ed'.

ontology.mental_model: Agent uses 'could have' + past participle to conceptualize a past possibility that did not occur or is uncertain.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Talking about past possibilities
ontology.agency_or_distance: Distance: looking back at an alternative past

positives: In fact it could have been dangerous.
What could have happened?
negatives: I could have a dog if I wanted.
We could have dinner after that.

can_do_statement: Can used affirmative 'could' have + '-ed' to talk about past possibility.

ontology.mental_model: Agent reflects on alternative outcomes or missed opportunities using abstract or passive subjects.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Alternative past outcomes
ontology.agency_or_distance: Distance: distancing from the actual past to explore a counterfactual

positives: her mother could have phoned her but she did not.
all these problems could have been avoided
negatives: I couldn't have bought it.
You could have asked me.

can_do_statement: Can use 'could have' + '-ed' to talk about regrets.

ontology.mental_model: Agent looks inward at their own past actions, expressing a counterfactual wish using 'I/we'.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Expressing personal regret
ontology.agency_or_distance: Distance: stepping back to evaluate one's own missed chances

positives: I wish I could have stayed, especially to help the children.
I could have listened more to my team members.
negatives: You could have given them better service.
It could have been dangerous.

can_do_statement: Can use 'could have' + '-ed' to speculate about the past.

ontology.mental_model: Agent posits theories about uncertain past events, typically involving third parties or hypotheticals (who, a thief, she).
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Theorizing about the past
ontology.agency_or_distance: Distance: distancing to deduce possible past realities

positives: I thought perhaps a thief could have entered my house.
who could have saved her?
negatives: I wish I could have stayed.
You could have given me more time.

can_do_statement: Can use 'could' as the past form of 'can' in reported speech.

ontology.mental_model: Agent uses 'could' within a subordinate clause to backshift 'can' to the past after a reporting verb.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Reporting past abilities or possibilities
ontology.agency_or_distance: Distance: temporal distance via reported speech backshifting

positives: I told them I couldn't go because I didn't have money
The woman said she could put me up if I wanted
negatives: Could you tell me the time?
I could hear what he said.

can_do_statement: Can use uncontracted 'not' for emphasis or in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using the full uncontracted 'not' to emphasize the negative point.

positives: Do not take on too many assignments at a time.
Keeping them in zoos will not help them.
negatives: Don't take on too many assignments.
I won't help them.

can_do_statement: Can use negative forms 'neither of' and 'none of' + pronoun or noun phrase with the affirmative form of the verb.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using neither of or none of with a pronoun

positives: Neither of us is liable in this case.
Moreover, none of my friends are interested.
negatives: Neither option is good.
I want none today.

can_do_statement: Can use 'neither … nor' to connect two words, phrases or clauses, often to give emphasis or focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Pairing neither and nor

positives: Neither you nor I would like that.
We can neither eat nor drink during the lessons.
negatives: I want neither of them.
Nor do I want this.

can_do_statement: Can use 'never' in front position followed by an inverted subject (most commonly 'I') + main verb, to give focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Inverting subject and verb after sentence-initial never

positives: Never have I seen such a realistic and impressive film before.
Never had I thought that my parents would do this to me.
negatives: I have never seen such a beautiful day.
Never give up on your dreams.

can_do_statement: Can form noun phrases with plural nouns + ' + noun.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: When a plural noun ending in 's' possesses something, you just add an apostrophe after the 's'.

positives: He had promised that he would go to his grandparents' house this afternoon.
Our company is a digital company with 15 years' experience.
negatives: He would go to his grandmother's house this afternoon.
Our company has 15 years of experience.

can_do_statement: Can form noun phrases with noun + 'of' + possessive determiner + noun + '‘s', particularly with 'friend' or 'friends'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To show possession more elegantly, use 'a friend of my father's' instead of 'my father's friend'.

positives: The owner is a friend of my father's.
She is an acquaintance of my sister's.
negatives: The owner is my father's friend.
She is my sister's acquaintance.

can_do_statement: Can form complex noun phrases by using adjective phrases as postmodifiers to give more information about the noun.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Sometimes adjectives come after the noun they describe, especially when the adjective is part of a longer phrase.

positives: We went to an island full of different and exotic species.
They delivered a box completely ready for shipment.
negatives: We went to a full island of exotic species.
They delivered a ready box for shipment.

guideword: FORM: COMPLEX NOUN PHRASES WITH ADJECTIVES COMBINED WITH 'BUT'
can_do_statement: Can form an increasing range of complex noun phrases with more than one adjective combined with 'but'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To create a strong impression, you can use 'but' to link two contrasting adjectives before a noun.

positives: I was born in a small but beautiful city.
The smoke in the air had a strong but good smell.
negatives: I was born in a small city but it is beautiful.
The smoke was strong but good.

can_do_statement: Can use the '-ing' form of verbs as nouns in subject position.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using '-ing' verbs as the main subject of a sentence to talk about activities.

positives: Working until midnight every evening is not reasonable.
Driving in a city is stressful.
negatives: I am working until midnight every evening.
The morning is nice.

can_do_statement: Can use uncountable nouns without a definite article to refer to an abstract thing in general.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using abstract nouns at the start of a sentence without 'the' to talk in general terms.

positives: Television is more attractive because it has moving images.
Education is important to prevent you from being a dog on a leash!
negatives: The education I received was poor.
His music was amazing.

can_do_statement: Can use the passive infinitive affirmative and negative forms after an increasing range of main verbs, modal verbs, adjectives and nouns, in impersonal constructions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: General passive infinitive (affirmative and negative).

positives: It is an opportunity not to be missed.
The house is likely to be built soon.
negatives: I want to be rich.
She happens to be here.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect passive affirmative form.

ontology.mental_model: Passive action completed before a past point.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past perfect passive.

positives: The car had been repaired before we sold it.
I noticed the window had been broken.
negatives: The car had not been repaired.
The window has been broken.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect simple affirmative and negative forms with modal verbs to refer to the past.

ontology.mental_model: Past hypothetical or deduced passive state.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Modal perfect passive.

positives: The accident could have been avoided.
The money might not have been stolen.
negatives: The accident was avoided.
The money might be stolen.

can_do_statement: Can use the past continuous passive affirmative.

ontology.mental_model: Action in progress in the past acting upon the subject
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past continuous passive

positives: The building was being renovated.
I knew I was being watched by them.
negatives: The house is being painted.
They were being very loud.

can_do_statement: Can use past simple passive negative.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing negative state or action received by subject in past
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past simple passive negative

positives: The tickets were not sold out.
He wasn't invited to the party.
negatives: She is not given any help.
I did not like the movie.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect passive negative form.

ontology.mental_model: Negative action completed before another past point, received by subject
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past perfect simple passive negative

positives: The issue had not been resolved before the meeting.
We left because we hadn't been served.
negatives: The issue has not been resolved yet.
I had not been there before.

can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous passive affirmative with an increasing range of verbs.

ontology.mental_model: Action currently in progress acting upon the subject
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present continuous passive affirmative

positives: The new system is being tested right now.
Our calls are being recorded.
negatives: The system is not being tested.
The building was being painted.

can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous passive negative.

ontology.mental_model: Negative ongoing action in the present acting upon the subject
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present continuous passive negative

positives: The rules are not being followed properly.
It isn't being reviewed at the moment.
negatives: The rules are being followed.
They were not being monitored.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect passive affirmative form (often in the context of reporting).  ► reported speech

ontology.mental_model: Resultant state in the present from a past action acting upon the subject
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect simple passive affirmative

positives: I have been asked to lead the project.
A decision has been reached by the board.
negatives: I have not been asked about it.
I had been told previously.

can_do_statement: Can use the passive with modal verbs to evaluate or summarise.

ontology.mental_model: Evaluating or summarizing a situation using modals in passive voice
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Passive with modals for summary

positives: In conclusion, it can be seen that the trends are changing.
I think something must be done immediately.
negatives: The bike can be repaired later.
He should be working now.

guideword: FORM: WITH VERBS TAKING TWO OBJECTS, , WITH PREPOSITIONAL PHRASE
can_do_statement: Can use the passive with a range of tenses and verbs needing two objects (e.g. give, offer, sell) with the direct object in subject position and the indirect object in a prepositional phrase.

ontology.mental_model: Focus on the direct object as subject, shifting recipient to prepositional phrase
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Passive with two-object verbs and 'to' phrase

positives: The award was given to him by the mayor.
A discount will be offered to students.
negatives: I gave the book to her.
She is going to school.

can_do_statement: Can use the passive with 'will' to talk about the future.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Passive with will

positives: The room will be cleaned tomorrow.
You'll be notified of the decision soon.
negatives: She will be traveling to Paris.
They will build a new house.

can_do_statement: Can use the passive with modal verbs in a range of contexts, with a variety of subjects.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing necessity or possibility in passive
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Passive with modal verbs

positives: The software should be updated regularly.
The package might be delivered today.
negatives: I must be dreaming.
They would be happy to help.

guideword: FORM: WITH VERBS TAKING TWO OBJECTS.
can_do_statement: Can use the passive with a wide range of verbs needing two objects, putting the indirect object in subject position.

ontology.mental_model: Focus on the recipient by placing indirect object in subject position
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Passive of two-object verbs

positives: She was offered a great opportunity.
I have been given the necessary documents.
negatives: The documents were given to me.
He gave me a present.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect passive negative form (often in the context of reporting). ► reported speech

ontology.mental_model: Negative resultant state in the present
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect simple passive negative

positives: The keys haven't been found yet.
The equipment has not been tested properly.
negatives: The keys have been found.
I haven't been feeling well.

can_do_statement: Can use have + object + -ed to talk about something where the speaker is in a pro-active or a passive role.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'have something done' to talk about arranging a service or experiencing something negative.

positives: I had my car serviced and visited Washington
I had my purse stolen
negatives: I have finished my homework.
She had finally seen the movie.

can_do_statement: Can use a reflexive pronoun with the 'get'-passive.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using a reflexive pronoun (like 'yourself') with 'get' + past participle.

positives: you could get yourself killed if you don't drive carefully enough.
he uses it to get himself involved in illegal activities.
negatives: I got myself a new car.
He got himself out of the room.

can_do_statement: Can use 'get' + object + 'to'-infinitive to talk about causing someone to do something.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'get someone to do something' to talk about persuading or causing someone to act.

positives: in order to get them to visit us more frequently.
It is a good way to get them to shop at this particular store.
negatives: I got a nice present from my parents.
She got into trouble at school.

can_do_statement: Can use the past continuous with a wide range of adverbs in the normal mid position.

ontology.mental_model: Modifying past ongoing action with complex adverbs.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past continuous + wistfully/increasingly/etc.

positives: My brother was constantly bothering me.
She was wistfully walking in the dusk.
negatives: He was always dreaming.
I was just watching.

can_do_statement: Can use the past continuous to make a request or suggestions more polite or less direct.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: I was wondering/thinking/hoping

positives: I was wondering if you could help me with this.
We were hoping you might join us for dinner.
negatives: I wonder if you could help me.
They are hoping to see you soon.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: had not been doing

positives: She had not been sleeping well lately.
I hadn't been waiting long when the bus arrived.
negatives: She had been sleeping well lately.
I haven't been waiting long.

guideword: FORM/USE: BACKGROUND INFORMATION WITH TIME CONJUNCTION
can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect continuous after a time conjunction to give background information.

ontology.mental_model: Past perfect continuous after a time conjunction
ontology.pedagogical_hook: after/when we had been doing

positives: After we had been waiting for an hour, the train finally arrived.
When they had been arguing for ten minutes, I decided to leave.
negatives: We had been waiting for an hour when the train arrived.
After we waited for an hour, the train arrived.

guideword: FORM/USE: BACKGROUND INFORMATION WITH RELATIVE CLAUSE
can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect continuous in a relative clause to give background information.  ► relative clauses

ontology.mental_model: Past perfect continuous in relative clauses
ontology.pedagogical_hook: who had been doing

positives: The man who had been following us suddenly disappeared.
I found the book that had been missing for weeks.
negatives: The man had been following us.
The man who was following us disappeared.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect continuous to talk about events which started before a time in the past and which finished, but where the effects or results were still important at a point in the past.

ontology.mental_model: Past perfect continuous to show past results
ontology.pedagogical_hook: had been doing so/because

positives: We had been working very hard all morning so we were exhausted.
It had been snowing, because the ground was completely white.
negatives: We had been working very hard all morning.
We have been working very hard so we are exhausted.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect continuous with adverbs in the normal mid position.

ontology.mental_model: Past perfect continuous with mid-position adverbs
ontology.pedagogical_hook: had [adverb] been doing

positives: I had really been looking forward to this.
She had only been living there for a month.
negatives: I had been really looking forward to this.
I had not been looking forward to this.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect simple after 'because' to give explanatory information.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Providing background explanations with 'because' + past perfect

positives: I was driving on to my parents' house because I had arranged to have dinner with them.
He was sleeping but I realised that this was because he had lost a lot of blood.
negatives: I am doing this because I have lost my keys.
We stayed inside because it had a bad smell.

guideword: FORM/USE: AFTER 'IF ONLY' AND 'WISH', IMAGINED PAST
can_do_statement: Can use the affirmative form after 'if only', and the affirmative and negative forms after 'wish' to talk about regret.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Regret over past events with 'wish' or 'if only' + past perfect

positives: If only I had listened to my father when he warned me!
I wish I hadn't told Pat about my plans.
negatives: I wish I had a car right now.
If only she would listen to me.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect simple with a wide range of adverbs (including 'finally', 'recently', 'simply') in the normal mid-position.  ► adverbs

ontology.mental_model: Modifying prior completed actions with adverbials
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Mid-position adverbs between auxiliary 'had' and past participle

positives: He had finally achieved his goal after years of work!
She had suddenly woken up at that noise.
negatives: I had walked there quickly.
He had been a teacher recently.

can_do_statement: Can invert the subject and auxiliary verb with 'no sooner … than' to talk about something that happened immediately before something else, often in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Emphasising immediate sequence of past events via inversion
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Formal inversion: 'No sooner had I...' to add dramatic sequencing

positives: No sooner had I gone to bed than someone broke the door down.
But, no sooner had I got there than my classmates informed me.
negatives: I had no sooner finished my work than the bell rang.
We will leave no sooner than 8 PM.

can_do_statement: Can use question forms.

ontology.mental_model: Inquiring about events completed before a past reference point
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Question inversion with past perfect 'had'

positives: Had I made the same mistake twice?
The question was: Why had he done that?
negatives: I asked why he had done that.
Had a great time yesterday?

can_do_statement: Can invert the subject and auxiliary verb after 'never (before)' to talk about a unique event, often in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Emphasising uniqueness of a past experience through inversion
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Formal emphatic phrasing with 'Never had I...'

positives: Never had I been in such a ridiculous situation!
Never before had we seen such marvellous species of fish.
negatives: I had never been in such a situation.
She will never have time for that.

can_do_statement: Can leave out the subject before the past perfect simple where it is understood from the previous clause.

ontology.mental_model: Linking sequential facts while omitting redundant subjects
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Compound predicates sharing a single subject into the past perfect

positives: Simon was a very famous writer and had written ten best-sellers.
They were cold and had gone numb.
negatives: Simon was a writer and he had written ten best-sellers.
She smiled, and had a piece of cake.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect simple to report statements, where the main verb in the reporting clause is in the past simple.  ► reported speech

ontology.mental_model: Backshifting past facts into reported speech
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past simple reporting verb + past perfect reported clause

positives: She tried to explain what had happened, but she couldn't.
I looked at the address and I knew what had happened to my sister's postcard.
negatives: She says what had happened.
He explained what is happening now.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect simple to talk about situations which changed.

ontology.mental_model: Contrasting an earlier plan or state with a subsequent change
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past perfect of intention (planned/wanted) contrasting with 'but'

positives: We had planned to go to Switzerland, but unfortunately our car broke down.
At first she had wanted to make the first move but she wasn't quite convinced.
negatives: I had hoped she would come.
We planned to go to the park, but it rained.

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect simple in relative clauses to give background information.    ► relative clauses

ontology.mental_model: Adding preceding context via relative modifiers
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Relative pronoun + past perfect for background details

positives: It was Annika who had arranged a huge party for her.
He went to the hotel to find out who the person was that had sent him a mysterious letter.
negatives: She found the book which she bought yesterday.
Who had arranged this?

can_do_statement: Can use the past perfect simple to report questions, where the main verb in the reporting clause is in the past simple.  ► reported speech

ontology.mental_model: Backshifting past questions into reported speech
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past reporting verb + wh-word/if + past perfect

positives: I asked him who had given him my phone number.
He asked me if I had seen her somewhere.
negatives: I asked him who gave him my phone number.
She wondered what he is doing.

can_do_statement: Can use 'yes/no', 'wh-', tag and negative question forms with an increasing range of verbs.

ontology.mental_model: Seeking information about a completed past action.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Questions in past simple using did or didn't.

positives: Did you succeed in finding one?
Didn't you completely tell me that?
negatives: Do you succeed in finding one?
Haven't you told me that?

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form with a wide range of regular and irregular verbs.

ontology.mental_model: Events explicitly marked as not having occurred in the past.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'did not' or 'didn't' to talk about what didn't happen.

positives: I didn't hesitate when they asked me.
They did not fully understand the consequences.
negatives: I don't hesitate when I'm asked.
She doesn't fully understand it.

can_do_statement: Can use the past simple with a range of subordinating conjunctions, including 'as soon as', 'before', 'if', 'once', 'since', 'so', 'until', 'when', 'while'.

ontology.mental_model: Connecting past events in time or condition.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using conjunctions like 'before' or 'once' with past tense verbs.

positives: Before I came here, I was happy.
Once he got inside, he searched.
negatives: Before I come here, I am happy.
Once he gets inside, he searches.

can_do_statement: Can use a range of time adjuncts with the past simple.

ontology.mental_model: Grounding an event in a specific past time frame.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using past simple alongside distinct time markers like 'yesterday' or 'last year'.

positives: I worked as a helper last summer.
It happened to me last year.
negatives: I am working as a helper this summer.
It happens to me every year.

can_do_statement: Can use the past simple with 'I wondered' and 'I wanted' as politeness structures, when making polite requests and thanking.

ontology.mental_model: Using past tense forms to create social distance and sound more polite.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Saying 'I wondered' or 'I wanted' to make a polite request.

positives: I wondered if you could introduce me.
First of all, I wanted to thank you.
negatives: I wonder if you could introduce me.
First of all, I want to thank you.

can_do_statement: Can use the past simple after 'if' as a politeness structure, especially in letters and emails.

ontology.mental_model: Mitigating requests by framing them as hypothetical scenarios.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using the past simple after 'if' in formal contexts like letters.

positives: I think it would be very helpful if I told you my own case.
I would be grateful if you gave me this job.
negatives: I think it will be very helpful if I tell you.
I will be grateful if you give me this job.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect continuous with adverbs in the normal mid position.

ontology.mental_model: An ongoing activity with emphasis via a mid-position adverb.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Placing adverbs like 'just', 'already', 'also' between 'have' and 'been'.

positives: I have just been reading an article.
You have already been complaining about headaches.
negatives: I just read an article.
You already complained about headaches.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form.

ontology.mental_model: Denial of a continuing past-to-present action
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect continuous in negative form

positives: I haven't been working too hard lately.
The machine has not been running correctly.
negatives: I haven't seen her in a while.
She has been doing her homework.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect continuous to focus on a finished activity in the recent past but where the effects or results are still important or relevant.

ontology.mental_model: Recent continuous action whose effects are still visible
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect continuous for recent past effects

positives: The roads are wet because it has been raining.
I'm tired because I've been working all day.
negatives: I am working on a new project.
He had been running before the game started.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form with an increasing range of verbs.

ontology.mental_model: Forming questions in the present perfect with interrogative words.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To ask a question in present perfect, put 'have' or 'has' before the subject.

positives: But what have these animals done?
How has your family been?
negatives: What did these animals do?
How is your family?

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form of the present perfect simple with 'still' to emphasise that something that was expected to happen continues not to happen.  ► adverbs

ontology.mental_model: Emphasizing an unfulfilled expectation that persists to the present.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'still haven't' or 'still hasn't' to show frustration that something expected has not happened yet.

positives: I still haven't decided.
He still has not replied to my message.
negatives: I haven't decided yet.
I still don't know.

can_do_statement: Can use less frequent simple prepositions, often in a more formal, literary or business context.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Deploying rare or literary single-word prepositions for formal impact.

positives: A silent screaming was heard throughout the whole dark room.
So why don't you act upon my advice?
negatives: He is looking at the picture.
She is sitting on the big chair.

can_do_statement: Can use preposition + relative pronoun as complement, to avoid preposition stranding, often in formal contexts. ► Clauses: relative

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Bringing the preposition forward with the relative pronoun to elevate register and avoid stranding.

positives: You have a vacancy in which I am very interested.
Children need someone to whom they can talk.
negatives: Which book are you reading in the library?
I know the man who is standing over there.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of complex prepositions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Mastering diverse complex prepositions for nuance and organization.

positives: She did not say very much except for oh and yes.
I have many hobbies in addition to reading.
negatives: He is reading an interesting book.
I will gladly do it for you right now.

guideword: FORM/USE: WITH ADVERBS OF INDEFINITE FREQUENCY
can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous with an increasing range of adverbs of indefinite frequency, often to talk about surprising or undesirable situations or events.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present continuous with 'constantly' or 'forever'

positives: You are constantly interrupting me when I speak.
She is forever losing her glasses in this house.
negatives: She is always losing her glasses in this house.
I continuously monitor the system for errors.

guideword: FORM: INVERSION WITH 'NOT ONLY … BUT ALSO'
can_do_statement: Can use the inverted form of the past simple with auxiliary 'do', in the phrase 'not only … but also'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Inversion with 'not only ... but also'

positives: Not only do they save you filing time, but also they save office space.
Not only does it look nice but it's also full of places.
negatives: They not only save time, but also space.
Not only did they save you filing time, but also they save office space.

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple to summarise events or plot in a story or piece of history, often to give immediate dramatic interest.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present simple for stories (takes place)

positives: The plot of the book takes place in Vienna.
The scene takes place on a train.
negatives: The meeting took place yesterday.
We are taking our places now.

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple with a wide range of speech act verbs, including '(dis)agree', 'accept', 'advise'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Wide range of speech act verbs

positives: We disagree with the new numbering system.
I advise you to take a coat.
negatives: I agreed with him.
They are advising us to leave.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'ours' with singular and plural reference, in object positions, and complement positions after 'be' and after prepositions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possessive pronouns in object position

positives: They told us we should bring ours.
This big house is actually ours.
negatives: Ours is the fastest car in the race.
We parked our car outside.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronouns 'hers' and 'ours' in comparative clauses.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Comparative with ours/hers

positives: Your project is much better than ours.
Her score was not as high as hers.
negatives: That book is ours.
She is as tall as him.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'ours' after noun + 'of'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Noun + of ours

positives: A good friend of ours will visit tomorrow.
Many competitors of ours are failing.
negatives: Some of our friends are coming.
They are friends of theirs.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'ours', with singular and plural reference, in subject position.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possessive pronoun ours as subject

positives: Ours is the only store open late.
I hope ours will be chosen.
negatives: The best idea was ours.
A friend of ours called today.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'hers', with singular reference, in object positions, and complement positions after 'be' and after prepositions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possessive pronoun hers as object

positives: She didn't realise the bag wasn't hers.
Pat happily gave hers to the guard.
negatives: Hers was a brilliant performance.
Her brother is coming over.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'theirs', with singular and plural reference, in object positions, and complement positions after 'be' and after prepositions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possessive pronoun theirs as object

positives: I can improve my language as well as theirs.
She told him the baby was theirs.
negatives: Theirs is a huge responsibility.
Their language is hard.

can_do_statement: Can use plural reflexive pronouns with 'by' to mean alone, without any help.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'by' + plural reflexive pronoun to mean 'alone'

positives: We are planning to spend a short holiday by ourselves.
The windows opened by themselves.
negatives: They did it themselves.
We looked at ourselves in the mirror.

can_do_statement: Can use the plural reflexive pronoun 'yourselves' for politeness.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'yourselves' for politeness instead of 'you'

positives: Training will be provided by yourselves.
Like yourselves, I am living in a busy town.
negatives: You enjoyed yourselves.
You cooked the food yourselves.

can_do_statement: Can use the singular pronoun 'itself' for emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'itself' for emphasis

positives: The story itself must be good.
The building itself looks splendid.
negatives: It opened by itself.
The process repeats.

can_do_statement: Can use plural reflexive pronouns after prepositions where the object of the preposition is the same as the subject of the verb.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using plural reflexives after prepositions

positives: It can help us to feel good about ourselves.
They didn't have enough time for themselves.
negatives: They opened by themselves.
We entertained ourselves.

guideword: FORM: SAME SUBJECT AND OBJECT, PLURAL
can_do_statement: Can use plural reflexive pronouns to refer to actions where the subject and object of the verb are the same.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using plural reflexives as verb objects

positives: We will be able to enjoy ourselves.
Adults often ask themselves the question.
negatives: We did the work ourselves.
They went by themselves.

can_do_statement: Can use plural reflexive pronouns for emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using plural reflexives for emphasis

positives: Cars themselves are never dangerous.
We ourselves don't know the answer.
negatives: They taught themselves how to play.
We traveled by ourselves.

can_do_statement: Can use the reflexive pronoun 'itself' with 'by' to mean alone or without any help.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'itself' with 'by' to mean 'alone'

positives: The window opened by itself.
An animal kept by itself will get lonely.
negatives: The building itself looks splendid.
He did it by himself.

can_do_statement: Can use the fixed expression 'in itself' as an intensifier .

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Focusing on the nature of the thing itself

positives: The idea in itself is quite remarkable.
A car can't be harmful in itself.
negatives: He was looking in the box itself.
I will be in soon itself.

can_do_statement: Can use 'it' as an object with 'make' to introduce something the speaker or writer is going to refer to.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'it' to setup an adjective

positives: They made it difficult to complain.
This will make it easier for everyone.
negatives: I made it myself.
We can make it to the party.

can_do_statement: Can leave out the subject pronoun with a limited range of verbs, in informal contexts. ► ellipsis

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Speaking quickly and informally

positives: Sounds great to me.
Got to go now.
negatives: The bells sounds great.
He got to go home.

can_do_statement: Can use 'one' as a generic personal pronoun in the subject position to mean people in general. ► generic pronouns

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Talking about people in general

positives: One must be careful.
If one wants to succeed, one must work hard.
negatives: I bought one apple.
She is the one I love.

can_do_statement: Can use dummy 'it' with 'appears', 'feels', 'looks' and 'seems'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Expressing impressions objectively

positives: It seems that we are lost.
It looks like a good idea.
negatives: He likes how it feels.
I don't know how it appears.

can_do_statement: Can use 'those' as a substitute, followed by a relative clause or '-ed' or '-ing'.

ontology.mental_model: Defining a subgroup using a demonstrative pronoun with a modifier
ontology.pedagogical_hook: those + relative clause/participle

positives: It is a good idea for those who are interested in sports.
All those attending are requested to be on time.
negatives: Those people who live there are very happy.
I want to read those books that you mentioned.

can_do_statement: Can use 'these ones', 'those ones' as a substitute for plural countable nouns that have previously been mentioned.

ontology.mental_model: Explicit substitution of plural countable objects
ontology.pedagogical_hook: these/those ones

positives: Let's just start with these ones.
I have got several of those ones.
negatives: I only need these two.
Those old ones are broken.

can_do_statement: Can use pronouns 'each', 'either', 'enough', 'neither', 'several' as subject and object pronouns.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'each', 'several', 'neither', or 'enough' as standalone pronouns

positives: Each has a unique style.
There are several that I like.
negatives: Each person has a unique style.
I like neither of them.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of pronouns ('neither', 'either', 'none') with 'of' followed by an object pronoun.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: referring to parts of a specific group using 'neither/either/none of'

positives: Neither of them knew.
We saw none of us.
negatives: Neither of the boys knew.
None of the cake is left.

can_do_statement: Can use 'these ones', 'those ones' as a substitute for plural countable nouns which have already been mentioned or are obvious from the context.

ontology.mental_model: Demonstrative substitution using 'these ones' or 'those ones'
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Saying 'these ones' or 'those ones'

positives: Let's just start with these ones.
Beside those ones, there's also an equal number of individuals.
negatives: These are good.
Those dogs are loud.

can_do_statement: Can use indefinite pronouns with a relative clause to form complex noun phrases, to give focus.

ontology.mental_model: Focusing on a specific aspect of an indefinite entity.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Modifying indefinite pronouns with a relative clause.

positives: Something that I really like is the food.
Everyone who can help should come.
negatives: I need something.
He is someone we met.

can_do_statement: Can use the full range of indefinite pronouns as subjects, with a singular verb.

ontology.mental_model: Full range of indefinite entities initiating action.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using indefinite pronouns as subjects with a singular verb.

positives: Everything is fine now.
Everybody tried to smile.
negatives: I saw everything.
He talked to everybody.

can_do_statement: Can use indefinite pronouns in vague expressions to refer to things in a non-specific way.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using phrases like 'or something', 'or anything like that'.

positives: We could go to the park or something.
I didn't have a cold or anything like that.
negatives: Do you want something?
I don't want anything.

can_do_statement: Can use 'we' and 'us' to refer to people in general.

ontology.mental_model: Collective human perspective including the speaker
ontology.pedagogical_hook: generic 'we' or 'us'

positives: We all know that being a writer is difficult.
Zoos give us different opportunities to understand nature.
negatives: We are going to the cinema tonight.
She gave us the tickets yesterday.

can_do_statement: Can use 'they/them' to refer back to indefinite pronouns when we do not know the number or gender.

ontology.mental_model: Anaphoric reference to a singular generic entity
ontology.pedagogical_hook: singular they

positives: If someone is watching a film that they don't like they can change the channel.
If anyone wishes to make any presentation they can contact Mr. Hari.
negatives: Someone is at the door, but he is hiding.
They went to the park and met someone there.

can_do_statement: Can use 'he/she', 'he' or 'she' or 'they' to refer back to gender neutral singular nouns or indefinite pronouns when we are not sure of the gender.

ontology.mental_model: Exhaustive anaphoric reference to unspecified gender
ontology.pedagogical_hook: he or she / he/she

positives: If a child had free time, he/she would play on his/her own.
If somebody wants to be a journalist, he or she has to have knowledge.
negatives: He loves her very much.
Is it for him or her?

can_do_statement: Can use 'one another' as the object of a verb or complement of a preposition to talk about the mutual behaviour of two or more people, often in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using formal 'one another'

positives: They can meet one another there.
We talk to one another every day.
negatives: One should help another person.
I saw one, and then another.

guideword: FORM/USE: TAGS WITH IMPERATIVES AS SOFTENERS
can_do_statement: Can use an affirmative or negative tag after an imperative clause to soften the imperative.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using tags to soften commands

positives: Think about it, will you?
Let's check together, shall we?
negatives: You will go to the store, won't you?
We shall overcome, shall we?

guideword: FORM: NEGATIVE QUESTIONS WITH MAIN VERBS
can_do_statement: Can use 'wh-'words + the negative form of auxiliary 'do' + subject + main verb to form 'wh-'questions.

ontology.mental_model: Inquiring about the absence of an action or challenging a failure to act
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To ask why something hasn't happened or isn't happening using negative forms of 'do'

positives: Why didn't you say something about it?
Why don't you go to your doctor?
negatives: I don't know why you didn't say something.
She asked why he didn't check.

can_do_statement: Can modify the reporting verb with an adverb.

ontology.mental_model: Modifying a reporting verb with an adverb to express the manner of speech.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Describing how someone said something.

positives: "I won't do it," she said forcefully.
He asked curiously about the details.
negatives: She quickly finished the work.
I suddenly thought of an idea.

guideword: FORM: DIRECT SPEECH, REPORTING CLAUSE, MID POSITION
can_do_statement: Can report speech and thought directly using the reporting verb in the mid position of the reported clause.

ontology.mental_model: Interrupting a direct quote with the reporting clause in the middle.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Putting the "he said" part in the middle of a quote.

positives: "No problem", I thought, "there is only one person".
"Forgive me", he said, "I will never leave."
negatives: "No problem, there is only one person," I thought.
He said, "Forgive me, I will never leave."

guideword: FORM: DIRECT SPEECH, REPORTING CLAUSE, INVERTED SUBJECT
can_do_statement: Can report speech directly inverting the subject and verb in the reporting clause where the subject is a proper noun or noun phrase.

ontology.mental_model: Reporting speech using verb-subject order when the subject is a noun phrase.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using "said John" instead of "John said" after a quote.

positives: "I was astonished", said John.
"Who are you?" asked Peter.
negatives: "I was astonished," John said.
John said he was astonished.

can_do_statement: Can use the past continuous of the reporting verb to report mental processes, with a finite or non-finite 'wh-'clause in the reported clause.

ontology.mental_model: Reporting a continuous past mental state or process.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using past continuous (was wondering, was thinking) to report thoughts.

positives: I was wondering why I failed.
While he was thinking how to reply, she left.
negatives: I wondered why I failed.
He was walking down the street.

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple form of the reporting verb to report information from a written source and a present tense verb in the reported clause.

ontology.mental_model: Reporting information from written sources as an enduring fact using present simple.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'says' or 'tells' to talk about what's written in a book, sign, or article.

positives: The guidebook says that we can get there by train.
Your advertisement tells us about the hotel.
negatives: He says he is coming.
The book was very interesting.

guideword: FORM: REPORTED REQUESTS AND COMMANDS, NEGATIVE
can_do_statement: Can report requests and commands with 'ask' or 'tell' + direct object + 'not' + 'to-'infinitive.

ontology.mental_model: Reporting a negative directive using not + to-infinitive.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Reporting negative commands like 'told him not to do it'.

positives: She told me not to be scared.
I asked Pat not to tell anyone.
negatives: She told me to be careful.
I asked him not for money, but for advice.

can_do_statement: Can report speech about events in the past with backshifts for tenses and words relating to time.

ontology.mental_model: Backshifting tenses and temporal adverbs when reporting past events.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using past perfect in reported speech for events further in the past.

positives: She had told me the previous day that it was important.
I had told my friends the day before that I expected an A.
negatives: She told me yesterday that it was important.
I had told my friends that I liked the movie.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of verb + particle + preposition + noun or pronoun.

ontology.mental_model: Directing an action towards an entity using a three-part phrasal verb.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using a phrasal verb with three parts.

positives: I can look up to someone in admiration.
We sat down and came up with the craziest idea.
negatives: I looked up at the sky.
I faced up the card.

can_do_statement: Can use an adverb between the verb and the preposition.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: The adverb interrupts the verb and its attached preposition to emphasize manner.

positives: I want to learn how to deal properly with them.
I hope you will look carefully at the enclosed papers.
negatives: I want to deal with them properly.
Look at the papers carefully before signing.

can_do_statement: Can use verb + preposition, where the preposition is separated from its complement.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: In English, the preposition can be left behind at the end of the clause.

positives: Our clothes have to be clean and nice to look at.
But there is one difficulty which we should deal with.
negatives: Look at the beautiful painting on the wall.
Deal with the issue right now.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of phrasal verbs without an object.

ontology.mental_model: Describing complex, self-contained actions with advanced phrasal verbs.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using advanced phrasal verbs without an object.

positives: Some species are dying out.
The following day my grandpa didn't show up.
negatives: I will show it up.
We ended the relationship.

can_do_statement: Can use phrasal verbs + nouns as object + particle.

ontology.mental_model: Separating a phrasal verb with a full noun phrase.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Putting a noun between the verb and the particle.

positives: Another way is also to turn the computers off.
It was necessary to call the electrician up.
negatives: Turn off the computers.
Call up the electrician.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of phrasal verbs + particle + object.

ontology.mental_model: Keeping advanced phrasal verbs together before an object.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using an advanced phrasal verb with an object.

positives: I can build up the whole surroundings.
I couldn't put off my crossing.
negatives: I build the surroundings up.
I couldn't put my crossing off.

can_do_statement: Can use semi-modal auxiliary verbs, 'dare' and 'need'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using dare and need as modals

positives: You needn't worry about the cost.
She daren't speak to him again.
negatives: You don't need to worry about the cost.
He didn't dare to speak.

can_do_statement: Can introduce a new subject before the '-ing' form (using noun or object pronoun).

ontology.mental_model: linking verbs to new subjects executing gerunds
ontology.pedagogical_hook: verb + object pronoun/noun + ing form

positives: Do you mind me staying here?
I can't stand people shouting.
negatives: Do you mind staying here?
I can't stand the terrible shouting.

can_do_statement: Can follow some verbs with a 'to'-infinitive or an '-ing' form, with a change in meaning.

ontology.mental_model: differentiating meaning based on verb complements (infinitive vs gerund)
ontology.pedagogical_hook: verbs that change meaning (remember, forget, stop) + to/ing

positives: I remembered to lock the door.
He stopped smoking last year.
negatives: I remembered his strange name.
He stopped the rolling ball.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of verbs followed by an '-ing' form.

ontology.mental_model: Conceptualising actions as objects of verbs.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using a verb to describe the process of doing another verb.

positives: I couldn't stand being there.
We may consider offering bonus schemes.
negatives: I stand to win.
I avoid the car.

can_do_statement: Can use some verbs connected with the senses + direct object + an '-ing' form, to give emphasis to an ongoing activity.

ontology.mental_model: Emphasizing an ongoing activity through sensory perception.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Describing what you saw or heard happening.

positives: Then I heard someone screaming.
We cannot see them running.
negatives: I heard someone scream.
I saw the man in the street.

can_do_statement: Can use 'there' with other verbs with modal meaning + 'be' + complement.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: These verbs express necessity or future expectation of existence.

positives: I figured out that there had to be matches somewhere.
There is going to be a theatre performance.
negatives: There will be a great show tomorrow.
There are matches somewhere in the cabin.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of linking verbs with complements.

ontology.mental_model: Using a wide range of linking verbs (seem, appear, remain, taste, sound) with adjectival or nominal complements.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using more advanced linking verbs to describe states.

positives: It all seems very confusing.
The whole house appeared very unfamiliar.
negatives: He tasted the soup.
She appeared in the doorway.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of compound adjectives ('open-minded', 'above-mentioned', 'well-to-do', 'jaw-dropping')

ontology.mental_model: hyphen compresses a clause into a trait
ontology.pedagogical_hook: shrink the clause

positives: She is a very open-minded person.
That was a jaw-dropping performance.
negatives: He has an X-ray scan.
T-shirt sizes are listed online.

can_do_statement: Can modify gradable adjectives with extreme adverbs of degree ('absolutely', 'extremely', 'incredibly', 'totally') to intensify their meaning.

ontology.mental_model: extreme adverbs slam the scale to its end
ontology.pedagogical_hook: slam the top of the scale

positives: The test was extremely difficult.
She bought a totally different dress.
negatives: In our classes, homework is totally online.
It is totally useless.

can_do_statement: Can use the '–ed' form of a verb as an adjective, after a noun.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: noun + past-participle — distill a full relative clause into a compact modifier
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker compresses the relational structure into a property word

positives: The topics discussed were very interesting.
I read the report published yesterday.
negatives: This week we received a part of a machine.
The world is divided between the two nations.

can_do_statement: Can use a postmodifier to make the superlative stronger in the structure superlative + postmodifier + noun.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: the + superlative + noun + that/who/which/I/you/we — annotate the top member with a clause
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker appends a clause to sharpen the superlative target

positives: It is the best possible way to solve the problem.
This was the highest ever temperature recorded.
negatives: Because of the possible outcomes, we decided to wait.
The worst is that we have no choice.

can_do_statement: Can use a postmodifier to make the superlative stronger, in the structure superlative + noun + postmodifier ('possible', 'ever', 'by far').

ontology.mental_model: Maximizing the superlative scope to all available possibilities or time
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Adding postmodifiers like 'possible' or 'ever' to strengthen superlatives

positives: We want to present ourselves in the best way possible.
That is her greatest performance ever.
negatives: It is the best way.
It was her greatest performance in history.

sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of adverbs to indicate degrees of certainty.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: undoubtedly / undeniably / certainly / definitely / surely / presumably — high end of the certainty dial
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker marks the proposition as settled

positives: I will undoubtedly finish the project.
She is undeniably talented.
negatives: Well, but definitely I would rather not know when.
Next guy this one definitely not.

sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of stance adverbs (simply, truly, surely, apparently, naturally, surprisingly, inevitably, literally, exceptionally, frankly, clearly, amazingly, wisely, admittedly) to indicate an attitude or viewpoint, often in clause initial position.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: simply / truly / surely / apparently / naturally / surprisingly / inevitably — finer-grained stance markers
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker marks nuanced distance from the proposition

positives: Obviously, if we produce more, we can sell more.
Surprisingly, the weather was quite nice today.
negatives: And obviously it needs a lot of people.
The answer is obviously incorrect.

sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of adverbs with adjectives to express degree or intensity.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: completely / absolutely / extremely / totally / utterly / thoroughly — turn the adjective past every default
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker pushes the adjective to the upper extreme

positives: The outcome is highly likely.
He is a thoroughly good man.
negatives: Maybe totally 15 days.
I would rather not go there.

can_do_statement: Can use degree adverbs ('slightly', 'a bit', 'much') to modify comparatives.

ontology.mental_model: Fine-tuning the gap between two compared entities
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'slightly', 'a bit', or 'much' before a comparative like 'more' or 'better'.

positives: My Spanish is slightly more fluent than my English.
Their grandparents are much more experienced.
negatives: I am much better now at reading.
I like it very much.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of degree adverbs to modify a range of adverb types. ► adjectives ► adverb phrases: form

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Combine strong modifiers like 'incredibly' or 'reasonably' with other adverbs like 'fast' or 'well'.

positives: The attitude has almost completely changed.
The charity event went reasonably well.
negatives: It is incredibly beautiful.
I am fairly certain.

can_do_statement: Can post-modify adverbs with 'enough to intensify'.

ontology.mental_model: Evaluating situations as sufficiently surprising or notable
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Post-modifying adverbs with 'enough' to express attitude

positives: Surprisingly enough, management was very responsive.
Sadly enough, I wasn't able to find a job.
negatives: He is tall enough.
I have enough money.

can_do_statement: Can modify a wide range of adverbs with other adverbs.

ontology.mental_model: Fine-tuning adverbial meaning with high-register modifiers
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Modifying adverbs extensively for precise academic or professional tone

positives: The value will drop extremely rapidly.
We can achieve market penetration relatively quickly.
negatives: It is extremely good.
It was relatively cheap.

can_do_statement: Can post-modify adverbs with a complex prepositional phrase complement, to highlight information.

ontology.mental_model: Highlighting the scope of an evaluative adverb using prepositional frames
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using prepositional phrases after adverbs to target specific information

positives: Luckily for you, I kept notes.
Unfortunately for some of them, it was nightmarish.
negatives: Luckily, I kept notes for you.
Unfortunately, it was bad for them.

can_do_statement: Can use 'the best' as a superlative adverb + pronoun + ellipted 'can' or 'could'.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing maximal effort or peak ability.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Superlative adverb 'the best' with ellipted modals.

positives: I'm sorry to say that she is not the best of cooks but she tries the best she can.
On Thursday I did the best I could.
negatives: She is the best singer.
This is the best I have ever seen.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'NOT ONLY … BUT (ALSO)' WITH INVERSION, FOCUS
can_do_statement: Can combine clauses using 'not only' in front position followed by an inverted first clause + … 'but (also)' to introduce the second clause, to give focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Starting a sentence with 'not only' for dramatic effect

positives: Not only did they come, but many others attended.
And not only was he helpful but the students learned a lot.
negatives: He not only studies hard, but also plays well.
I only wanted to help.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'LET' + THIRD PERSON PRONOUN, PERMISSION, ORDER
can_do_statement: Can use an imperative clause with  'let' + 'him/her/them' + base form of a main verb, to  give permission or allow something or instruct someone to allow something.

positives: Let him decide what to do.
Let them have more free time.
negatives: They let him leave early.
Let us go to the park.

can_do_statement: Can use imperatives to point within or to a document within formal contexts, often academic.

positives: See enclosed brochure for further information.
Look at the graph below.
negatives: I will see you tomorrow at the office.
They looked at the picture on the wall.

can_do_statement: Can use an imperative clause with  'let' + 'him/her/them' + base form of a main verb, to disallow something or instruct someone to disallow something.

positives: Don't let them spend all their time playing games.
Don't let him go out alone.
negatives: He didn't let them enter.
Don't let me down.

can_do_statement: Can use imperatives to introduce a condition followed by 'and' to introduce a consequence of the condition.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Price Tag — hanging an automatic consequence off an order: do X, and Y follows.

positives: Send me the PDF and I will get it.
Do it and you will see the results.
negatives: And and and they're thirty.
Yeah, so they will and they're trolling.

can_do_statement: Can use non-finite clauses after 'if'. .► 'clauses: conditionals'

ontology.pedagogical_hook: if + VBN or VBG

positives: Please do not hesitate to ask for further assistance if needed.
There are some suggestions that, if taken, could improve the school.
negatives: If you need anything, let me know.
I don't know if he is coming.

can_do_statement: Can use a non-finite subordinate clause with an '-ed' form, before a main clause, to give focus.

ontology.mental_model: Fronting a participial phrase for discourse focus
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Fronted past participle clauses

positives: Compared to the campsite job this one has its advantages.
Based on the assessment above, I recommend some actions.
negatives: He based his theory on recent data.
They compared the two products carefully.

can_do_statement: Can introduce a subordinate clause with inverted 'should/had/were' + subject + verb, in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Inversion for counterfactuals or strong conditions
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Had we known... Should you need...

positives: Should you need any further assistance, contact me.
Had we known that before, we could have taken more money.
negatives: Should we leave now?
Had they already left when you arrived?

can_do_statement: Can use a non-finite clause, introduced by 'not' + '-ing', to give more information.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Not + -ing for background information

positives: Not knowing the North of London very well, it took me time.
Not having accepted his wife's death, the father is left alone.
negatives: He is not going to the party.
I preferred not doing anything yesterday.

can_do_statement: Can form ellipted 'if' clauses with 'if' + '-ed' form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'if' directly with an '-ed' verb.

positives: Furthermore I found little rooms where an employee could take a short nap if needed.
Meals are served, if requested, three times a day.
negatives: Meals are served if they are requested.
If I requested it, they would serve it.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'IF' + PAST PERFECT + MODAL VERBS IMAGINED SITUATION, REGRET
can_do_statement: Can form conditional subordinate clauses with if + the past perfect simple and modal verb + 'have' + '-ed' in the main clause, to talk about imagined situations in the past, often with regret.

ontology.mental_model: Counterfactual reasoning with various modals in the past.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'could have' or 'might have' with a past perfect 'if' clause.

positives: All this could have been avoided, if the plan had been more flexible.
If I had gone to another city, I might have had a different opinion.
negatives: I could have done it.
If I had time, I might go.

can_do_statement: Can form subordinate conditional clauses with 'if you should', in polite, formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'if you should' for formal situations.

positives: If you should have any concerns, please tell me.
If he should call, let me know.
negatives: You should go if you want.
If you want, you should go.

can_do_statement: Can introduce a conditional subordinate clause with 'should' + inverted subject.

ontology.mental_model: Hypothetical condition introduced by modal inversion
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'should' to mean 'if' in formal contexts

positives: Should you require any further information, please ask.
Should there be a lack of mutual understanding a break-up is unavoidable.
negatives: You should require more information.
I think you should go.

can_do_statement: Can use 'either … or' to combine more complex strings of clauses and sentences.

ontology.mental_model: Framing an exclusive choice between complex alternative scenarios.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'either...or' to present two entirely different complex options or plans.

positives: Either we leave for the station right now, or we will miss the last train home.
You can either stay here and wait for her, or you can go ahead and I will join you.
negatives: Either the blue one or the red one.
I don't want either.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'NOT ONLY … BUT ALSO' WITH INVERSION
can_do_statement: Can use inverted auxiliary 'do' + the subject after 'not only', to give focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: inversion for emphasis

positives: Indeed, not only did they teach us useful knowledge, but they also organised practical exercises.
Not only do I speak fluent English, but I also speak French.
negatives: He did not only do his homework, but he also washed the dishes.
Not only are they nice, they are also smart.

can_do_statement: Can use '(and) yet' to combine phrases and clauses to introduce a contrast, often unexpected.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: unexpected contrast

positives: The host family was carefully selected, yet it was four miles away.
I saw it, and yet it felt weird.
negatives: I haven't done it yet.
Are we there yet?

can_do_statement: Can use 'not only … but also' to combine phrases and clauses, often for focus or emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: combining clauses

positives: This book is not only a guide to the history of music but also a compendium of theory.
If we move we can not only solve the problems, but also gain other benefits.
negatives: Not only do I speak fluent English, but I also speak French.
Not only did they run, but they also hid.

can_do_statement: Can use 'whatever', 'wherever', 'however', etc. as a subordinating conjunction, at the beginning of a sentence, to give focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: focus subordinators

positives: Whatever you choose, you'll probably have to share it with other people.
Wherever you go, you find shops.
negatives: I'll do whatever it takes.
I'll go wherever you go.

can_do_statement: Can use 'one's' to indicate possession, referring to people in general.

ontology.mental_model: Mapping possession, quantification, or specific reference to an entity.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Identifying the scope or owner of a noun phrase.

positives: Tourism can affect one's life.
It depends on one's ability to communicate.
negatives: One is enough for me.
He's the only one.

can_do_statement: Can use 'either' and 'neither' + 'of' with plural noun phrases or pronouns.► pronouns

ontology.mental_model: Specification of alternative or negative inclusion from a specific plural set.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'either of' or 'neither of' before a group.

positives: Either of the measures is recommended.
