Neither of us could foresee the problem.
negatives: I don't like either.
Neither one is good.

can_do_statement: Can use determiners in hyperbole, often in informal contexts ('millions of', 'loads of', 'tons of').

ontology.mental_model: Exaggeration of quantity for rhetorical effect.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using hyperbole like 'millions of' or 'tons of'.

positives: I managed to fit in millions of cookbooks.
I received tons of plastic ducks.
negatives: I have a million things to do.
She has a heavy load to carry.

can_do_statement: Can use 'either' and 'neither' with singular nouns.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'either' or 'neither' directly before a singular noun.

positives: Neither party could foresee the rise.
Either way is possible.
negatives: I like neither of the parties.
We didn't go that way either.

can_do_statement: Can use a range of phrases as discourse markers to point to other parts of a text.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Navigating references within a document

positives: As mentioned earlier, we have already shipped the order.
The results are completely valid, as shown above.
negatives: He mentioned earlier that he would be late.
The painting above the fireplace is beautiful.

can_do_statement: Can use fixed expressions in the front position for focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using idiomatic frames for focus

positives: All in all, it was a fantastic experience.
All in all, the movie exceeded my expectations.
negatives: They were all in all the best players on the team.
I put my all in all my projects.

can_do_statement: Can use 'What' + noun or pronoun + verb phrase as subject + 'be', for focus.

ontology.mental_model: Clefting to highlight the object of desire/need
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Isolating the most important detail

positives: What we need is a better strategy for the team.
What I really want is a glass of cold water.
negatives: I do not know what we need to do.
What is the best way to handle this?

can_do_statement: Can use imperatives as pointing devices within texts for focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Commanding focus to a specific element

positives: Notice the difference in the shading techniques.
See the attached document for more details.
negatives: Did you notice the difference between them?
I want to see the latest figures tomorrow.

can_do_statement: Can use 'Wh-'cleft clauses as titles or subtitles, to point to something that follows, for focus.

ontology.mental_model: Using a question-like structure as a declarative title
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Framing topics dynamically

positives: Why I think this will work is another story.
How we can improve sales in the next quarter.
negatives: Why do you think this will work?
How can we improve sales in the next quarter?

can_do_statement: Can use a non-finite subordinate clause with an '-ed' form, before a main clause, for focus, often in formal, academic or business contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Setting conditions elegantly

positives: Compared to last year, our profits have doubled.
Outlined below are the main reasons for our decision.
negatives: We compared our results to last year's figures.
The proposal outlined below needs review.

can_do_statement: Can use the future continuous with 'might' or 'may' to talk about an event or activity potentially in progress at a specified or understood time in the future.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing uncertainty about an action in progress in the future
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'might be -ing' or 'may be -ing' for possible future actions.

positives: The new offerings might be coming up shortly.
Your boss may be calling at 10 pm tonight.
negatives: They will be coming soon.
Your boss may call later.

can_do_statement: Can use the future perfect with adverbs (in the normal mid-position).

ontology.pedagogical_hook: adding an adverb mid-sentence for future perfect

positives: You will surely have discovered why this man is famous.
Sales will possibly have fallen again by the end of the year.
negatives: You will have successfully discovered it.
I will have learned it by tomorrow.

can_do_statement: Can use the future perfect simple with 'will' to make assumptions about the present, particularly with 'you'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'will have done' to guess what has happened

positives: As you will have heard, this year's programme was a success.
All of this is because her book will have included the traditions.
negatives: You will have finished by tomorrow.
I will not have done it.

can_do_statement: Can use the future perfect simple with 'will' as a politeness strategy, often in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using future perfect simple to soften a statement and sound polite in formal contexts.

positives: I hope I will have reassured you by the end of this letter.
I trust we will have clarified the situation sufficiently.
negatives: I have reassured you many times.
I will reassure you soon enough.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form 'shall not'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'shall not' for formal negative statements.

positives: We shall not forget to mention the legal consequences.
My client shall not release you from the agreement.
negatives: We shall forget about it.
Will they not release you?

can_do_statement: Can use 'be' + 'going to' with an increasing range of adverbs (particularly adverbs of certainty) in the normal mid position.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using future constructs to indicate forthcoming actions or states.
ontology.agency_or_distance: Agency via intention; Distance via forward-looking temporal projection.

positives: He is probably going to finish soon.
It is undoubtedly going to have an effect.
negatives: I am going to probably finish soon.
He is going to surely try.

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple with 'by the time' to refer to the future.

ontology.mental_model: future event relative to a deadline
ontology.pedagogical_hook: present simple with 'by the time'

positives: By the time he gets home, he will want to sleep.
By the time you arrive the office will be closed.
negatives: By the time he arrived, it was dark.
He had left by the time we got there.

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple after speech act verbs expressing suggestions and obligation.

ontology.mental_model: imposing obligation or offering formal suggestion
ontology.pedagogical_hook: present simple/subjunctive after suggestion verbs

positives: We would suggest that our management takes a closer look.
I recommend that we go to the theatre.
negatives: I suggested that we left early.
I strongly recommend going there.

can_do_statement: Can modify adjectives with adverbs, often for emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Adding strong emphasis to assertions

positives: It is painfully obvious that it will rescue our city.
It is highly unlikely that the goods can vanish.
negatives: It is very possible that they win.
It is quite probable that it rains.

can_do_statement: Can modify adjectives with degree adverbs, often to make an assertion less direct.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Softening assertions with degree adverbs

positives: There's a public transport strike which is quite probable.
It is almost certain that we'll have fights.
negatives: It is highly unlikely that it happens.
It is totally certain.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of adverbs with 'can' in the normal mid position after the modal verb). ► adverbs

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using complex adverbs like fully, honestly with 'can'

positives: I can honestly say that I know her well.
Only then can you fully understand the situation.
negatives: I can run fast.
She fully can comprehend it.

can_do_statement: Can use expressions with 'can' or 'can’t' to give focus or add emphasis, such as 'as you can see', 'I can't say', 'I can tell you that', 'as you can imagine', 'I can say that', 'I can assure you that'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using fixed phrases like 'as you can see' for emphasis

positives: As you can imagine, it was a very difficult time.
I can tell you that we worked really hard.
negatives: I can swim.
She can say what she wants.

can_do_statement: Can use 'can' in passive reporting clauses in a more formal impersonal style (e.g. for reports and academic contexts), such as 'It can be said that', 'It can be argued (that)', 'It can be concluded that', 'It can be considered'.► passives

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'it can be + V3' in academic contexts

positives: It can be argued that the policy failed.
Taking everything into account, it can be concluded that it is useful.
negatives: I can be ready in five minutes.
This box can be moved easily.

can_do_statement: Can use 'can't' or 'cannot have' + '-ed' to make deductions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'can't have + V3'

positives: We can't have used so much electricity.
It cannot have been a disappointment.
negatives: I can't have a break now.
They cannot have this item.

can_do_statement: Can use the fixed expression 'I dare say' to say that something is probably true.

ontology.mental_model: Agent uses the fixed phrase 'I dare say' to cautiously assert probability or likely truth.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Softly asserting probability
ontology.agency_or_distance: Distance: softening a claim through an epistemic framing device

positives: I dare say that the last option may be the best one.
which I dare say needs improvement.
negatives: I dare you to say that to his face.
I didn't dare to speak.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Ask about boldness

positives: Dare we ask for more time?
Dare anyone challenge the new rules?
negatives: I dare you to jump over that fence.
How dare you speak to me like that!

can_do_statement: Can use 'how dare … !' to express disapproval or offense about something

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Expressing indignation

positives: How dare they cancel the show!
How dare you come into my house!
negatives: Dare you tell her the truth?
I dare say she is right.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be' + 'not' + adjective + 'that-' clause to make an assertion less direct.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be not adjective that

positives: I am not sure that it will work.
It isn't likely that they will come.
negatives: I am sure that it is not true.
She is not the one that I saw.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be set to' to talk about strong assertion about the future, especially in institutional contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be set to

positives: The population is set to increase.
We are set to leave.
negatives: The table is set to perfection.
He set the dial to five.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may not have' + '-ed' to talk about possibility in the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: may not have + past participle

positives: It may not have been the best idea.
They may not have obtained the results yet.
negatives: I may not have the time for this.
He may not be coming.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may well' to give emphasis to something unexpected.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: When something is very likely, you can say it 'may well' happen.

positives: I think they may well come to an agreement.
It may well be that after leaving school they become our employees.
negatives: He may do well on the exam.
The well may dry up.

can_do_statement: Can use 'might not have' + '-ed'.

ontology.mental_model: Possibility with a past reference in negative form
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past hypothetical negative

positives: She might not have realised the time.
They might not have seen it.
negatives: She might not have time to go.
They might have seen it.

can_do_statement: Can use 'might not have' + '-ed' to talk about possibility with a past reference.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing that something possibly didn't happen
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past possibility

positives: It might not have been a good idea.
He might not have finished yet.
negatives: He might not have enough money.
It might have been lost.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possibility questions

positives: Might it be a good idea?
Might they have left?
negatives: It might be a good idea.
They might have left.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form to make polite criticisms and suggestions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Polite suggestions

positives: Might I suggest an alternative?
Might it not be wise to wait?
negatives: It might be wise to wait.
I might suggest an alternative later.

can_do_statement: Can use 'might' followed by 'but' to console or justify.

ontology.mental_model: Conceding a point before making a contrast
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Concession and contrast

positives: It might be hard, but it's worth it.
You might not agree, but I have to do this.
negatives: It might be hard.
But you might not agree.

can_do_statement: Can use 'needn't have' + '-ed'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past action that happened but wasn't necessary

positives: You needn't have bought me anything!
We needn't really have bothered.
negatives: You didn't need to buy me anything.
I don't need to have a reason.

guideword: FORM/USE: DESIRED STATES, WITH 'THERE OUGHT TO BE'
can_do_statement: Can use 'there ought to be' to talk about desired states of affairs.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Combining existential 'there' with 'ought to be'

positives: I think there ought to be more excursions.
There ought to definitely be a lift in this building.
negatives: It ought to be easier than this.
There should be more excursions.

can_do_statement: Can use 'ought to' with 'really' to add emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Adverbial intensification with 'really'

positives: We really ought to think a little bit more about it.
You really ought to ask for details.
negatives: We ought to really think about it.
You really should ask for details.

can_do_statement: Can use 'ought to' to talk about something which is likely.

ontology.mental_model: High probability based on logical deduction
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using obligation modal for likelihood

positives: It ought to provide useful information.
You ought not to be hungry.
negatives: He should provide information.
I bought it to provide relief.

can_do_statement: Can use 'ought to have' + '-ed' to refer to desired states of affairs in the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using perfect infinitive for past unreality

positives: We ought to have booked one!
The government ought to have known that.
negatives: We ought to book one.
I think you ought to have a look.

can_do_statement: Can use 'shall' to express commands in very formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Absolute obligation or directive, often legalistic.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Formal rule or command.

positives: The contract shall be binding.
Tenants shall pay on the first.
negatives: Shall we dance?
I shall see him tomorrow.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form.

ontology.mental_model: Explicitly negating future event or permission.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'Shall not' for formal negation.

positives: They shall not pass.
Students shall not run in the halls.
negatives: I shall pass.
We shall go.

can_do_statement: Can use 'should' after 'if' to talk about possible situations in the future.

ontology.mental_model: Describing a hypothetical future condition with a low probability.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Just in case... Say 'If you should need anything'.

positives: If you should change your mind and prefer to take a taxi, call us.
If something should happen, call 112.
negatives: You should change your mind if you want to.
He should call 112 if something happens.

can_do_statement: Can use 'should' with an inverted subject to refer to possible situations, in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: A highly formal, conditional structure replacing 'if'.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Write a formal letter: 'Should you need assistance, please call'.

positives: Should you need any further information, don't hesitate to contact us.
Should you withhold any important information, this could stop payment.
negatives: You should need any further information.
Why should you withhold important information?

can_do_statement: Can use the question form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Questions about past habits

positives: What did we use to eat?
Did she use to live here?
negatives: We didn't use to eat there.
I used to eat a lot.

can_do_statement: Can use 'will' to talk about something which is typical or habitual.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'will' to describe habitual actions

positives: She will often knock on the door before entering.
They won't usually allow outside food.
negatives: I will go there tomorrow.
I usually knock on the door.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of adverbs with 'would', including 'strongly', 'easily', 'especially', 'actually', 'absolutely', 'gladly'  ► adverbs

ontology.mental_model: Modifying 'would' with an increasing range of adverbs.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'would strongly recommend', 'would easily fit'.

positives: I would strongly recommend the following changes.
Nascha would easily fit into a family.
negatives: I strongly recommend it.
I would really like it.

can_do_statement: Can use 'not necessarily' as a short response.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Politely disagreeing or doubting

positives: Thinking of Christmas? Not necessarily.
Does that mean we lose? Not necessarily.
negatives: It is not necessarily true.
That does not necessarily mean anything.

can_do_statement: Can use 'not necessarily' to express a possible exception to a general perception, i.e. not in every case.

ontology.mental_model: Speaker signals that a common assumption is not universally true.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'not necessarily' to show that something isn't always the case.

positives: Bigger isn't necessarily better.
That does not necessarily mean he is guilty.
negatives: It is necessarily a bad idea.
They did not leave the room.

can_do_statement: Can use 'could have' + '-ed' form to express disapproval or criticism.

ontology.mental_model: Agent directs disapproval toward another entity (usually 'you' or 'they') for failing to perform a desired past action.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Criticizing past inaction
ontology.agency_or_distance: Agency: asserting normative expectation on another's past behavior

positives: I think that you could have arranged entertainment.
you could have given them a better service
negatives: I could have done that if I had time.
It could have been worse.

can_do_statement: Can use 'whatsoever' after a negative form for emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasizing negation with whatsoever

positives: We have no experience whatsoever.
There shall be no implication whatsoever for their rights.
negatives: I will do whatever you ask.
There is someone who can help.

can_do_statement: Can use auxiliary 'do' + inverted subject after 'not only', to give focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Inverting subject and do/does/did after not only

positives: Not only do they have the biggest turnover, they also increased it.
Not only did we lose the match, but we also lost our best player.
negatives: We not only do our homework, but we also study.
They not only did the work, but they also checked it.

can_do_statement: Can use 'not' + stance adverb, often  in a mid position, to soften the directness of a statement.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Softening negatives with stance adverbs

positives: This is not necessarily the way the older generation would see it.
Organising the entertainment is not really my thing.
negatives: I am necessarily going to be late.
It is actually quite warm today.

can_do_statement: Can use negative pronoun 'none' to substitute for subject and object pronouns or noun phrases. ► pronouns: substitution

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using none to replace a noun

positives: Problems when using English? None.
I asked for apples but there were none.
negatives: None of the students were there.
I like none of these options.

can_do_statement: Can use 'not with indefinite pronouns 'everyone' and 'everything' and determiners 'every', 'all'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using not before all, every, everyone, or everything

positives: Not everyone likes sports or music.
Not all students can attend the centre.
negatives: They did not always agree.
I will not ever see him again.

can_do_statement: Can use '(very) few' meaning 'not many' to refer to people in formal written contexts, often reports or surveys.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using few as a pronoun for people

positives: They were sent to Britain but few had any real contact.
Everyone tried to conquer them, but few managed.
negatives: Very few people know the truth.
I have a few questions for you.

guideword: FORM: NOUN PHRASE WITH POSSESSIVE 'S WITHOUT NOUN
can_do_statement: Can form complex noun phrases with noun phrase + 'of' + noun phrase + possessive determiner ''s', omitting the noun where it is previously mentioned.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: If the noun is obvious from context, you can drop it after an apostrophe 's'.

positives: Our team is faster than our competitors'.
I think it would be better to include a student's view of the college, not only a teacher's.
negatives: Our team is faster than our competitors' team.
I think it would be better to include a student's view, not only a teacher's view.

can_do_statement: Can use nominalised forms in academic or business contexts, to make something more formal.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: In formal or academic writing, turn verbs into nouns (nominalisation) for a more professional tone.

positives: The output in state-owned industry increased by 12%.
We noted the fluctuations in industrial output.
negatives: The industry produced state-owned items.
They fluctuated industrially.

can_do_statement: Can form complex noun phrases with 'wh-' cleft clauses, followed by 'be', to give focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Start a sentence with a 'What...' clause followed by 'is' or 'was' to place strong focus on the information that comes next.

positives: What everyone loved were the special effects.
What companies care about is money.
negatives: Everyone loved the special effects.
Companies care about money.

can_do_statement: Can use the '-ing' form of verbs as abstract nouns.

ontology.mental_model: Abstract processes or activities conceptualized as entities
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Gerunds acting as abstract nouns, often as subjects.

positives: Learning English is fun.
Advertising is expensive.
negatives: I am learning English.
They are teaching math.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of uncountable nouns, particularly referring to abstract concepts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using uncountable nouns for complex, abstract ideas like humanity or solidarity.

positives: Through that we can develop more humanity, solidarity, tolerance and respect among people of different countries.
Above all, the administration is not very efficient.
negatives: I have three apples.
He drove the car.

can_do_statement: Can use a passive non-finite '-ing' form as a subordinate clause or a noun clause to give explanatory background information.

ontology.mental_model: Backgrounding agent in non-finite continuous clause
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Passive non-finite -ing form

positives: Being invited to the conference was an honor.
Being completely exhausted by the hike, we rested for an hour.
negatives: He is being annoying today.
She enjoys being a mother.

can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous passive negative form to refer to ongoing situations in the present.

ontology.mental_model: Action ongoing in present being negated.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present continuous passive with negation to show lack of current action.

positives: The store is not being promoted enough.
They aren't being seen as equals.
negatives: The store is being promoted well.
They have not been seen.

can_do_statement: Can use the passive with 'it' as a dummy subject, to summarise or evaluate in discussions, usually in formal or academic writing.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'it' passive to evaluate.

positives: It can be concluded that the project was a success.
It has been found that these products are safe.
negatives: The manual can be concluded by reading it.
He has been found in the woods.

can_do_statement: Can use 'get' + object + '-ed' to talk about causing or instructing something to happen or to be done by somebody else, often informally.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'get something done' to casually talk about causing something to happen.

positives: she is always the one who tries to get things done.
it took hours to get it repaired.
negatives: I got to go to the store.
She got a new book for her birthday.

can_do_statement: Can use 'get' + object + '-ing' to talk about causing someone or something to do something.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Causing action (get someone doing something).

positives: The speech really got me thinking about my future.
The lively music got the audience dancing immediately.
negatives: I got going early in the morning.
I finally got my painting back from the gallery.

can_do_statement: Can invert the subject and affirmative auxiliary verb to talk about imagined situations in the past, often with regret, in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Inverted 3rd conditionals: 'Had I known...'

positives: Had I known the tour would be so bad, I wouldn't have booked it.
Sometimes I think that had I gone to Britain without this experience, my life would be different.
negatives: Had I known the answer?
If I had known the tour would be so bad, I wouldn't have booked it.

guideword: FORM: INVERSION WITH 'NOT ONLY … BUT ALSO'
can_do_statement: Can use the inverted form of the past simple with auxiliary 'do', in the phrase 'not only … but also'.

ontology.mental_model: Adding rhetorical emphasis by fronting the negative particle.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Inverting subject and auxiliary after 'Not only'.

positives: Not only did I find them, but also others.
Not only didn't we travel, but also we stayed.
negatives: I not only found them, but also others.
We not only travelled, but also stayed.

can_do_statement: Can use the past simple with 'did' for emphasis.

ontology.mental_model: Asserting truth or contrasting with an expectation.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'did' before the main verb for emphasis.

positives: We did reach the target figure.
It is true that it did rain during the day.
negatives: Did we reach the target figure?
I didn't reach the target figure.

can_do_statement: Can use 'yes/no', 'wh-', tag and negative question forms with a wide range of verbs.  ► Questions

ontology.mental_model: Requesting information about past events with a wide range of verbs.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Forming questions confidently with 'did' or 'didn't'.

positives: Did you spot the fact?
How did it turn out then?
negatives: Do you spot the fact?
How does it turn out then?

guideword: USE: COMPLEX ORDERING OF PAST EVENTS
can_do_statement: Can use the past simple to order sequences of events in the past in a complex way.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using forms like 'following' or 'after having' to order events.

positives: Following advice from a friend, I purchased the product.
After having discussed this, we came up with decisions.
negatives: I purchased the product.
We came up with decisions.

can_do_statement: Can use the past simple 'I thought' as a politeness structure to sound less direct.

ontology.mental_model: Using the past tense of think to soften statements.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'I thought' to make a suggestion sound less direct.

positives: I thought it would be a good idea.
I thought you might be interested.
negatives: I think it would be a good idea.
I think you might be interested.

can_do_statement: Can use the full negative forms with a wide range of verbs, often in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Formal denial of an action that was expected or possible up to the present.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: In formal writing, use the full 'have not' instead of 'haven't'.

positives: Thus, you have not fulfilled your task with due care.
Somehow, education has not evolved in my country.
negatives: Thus, you haven't fulfilled your task.
Education hasn't evolved.

can_do_statement: Can use less frequent complex prepositions, often in a more formal, literary or business context.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Deploying rare, multi-word prepositional phrases to specify precise relationships in formal text.

positives: They are so ahead of their time.
I stayed home on account of the bad weather.
negatives: He created a new account of his own.
I was completely out of it today.

can_do_statement: Can use question forms to ask rhetorical questions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Rhetorical questions using present continuous

positives: Why are we becoming shallow over something so trivial?
Why is technology taking over our lives?
negatives: Why do you leave so early?
How did they fix the roof?

can_do_statement: Can use the negative question form as a persuasion strategy.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Negative questions for persuasion

positives: Don't you just hate taking the bus to school every morning?
Don't you find that when you are having a shower or bath, you occasionally run out of water?
negatives: You don't just hate taking the bus, do you?
Why didn't you just hate taking the bus?

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple with a wide range of reporting verbs, especially in academic contexts, including 'demonstrate', 'illustrate'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Academic reporting verbs

positives: The popularity of this TV game in Russia clearly demonstrates the nature of human fears.
The charts illustrate the number of employees.
negatives: The study demonstrated the effect.
He is illustrating the book.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative question form to check opinions.

ontology.mental_model: Checking or confirming an opinion using a negative question.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Checking opinions using negative questions.

positives: Doesn't it really sound like a good idea?
Don't you think we should go now?
negatives: I don't think it sounds good.
You do not like it at all.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'ours', in subject position.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possessive pronoun ours as subject

positives: Ours was absolutely breathtaking.
I hope they improve conditions as ours did.
negatives: The largest garden is ours.
We are proud of our garden.

can_do_statement: Can use 'it' with the passive voice where the subject is unknown or unimportant, often in formal contexts. ► passives

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Formal passive with 'it'

positives: It is hoped that this report will help the club.
It was considered to be the most important thing.
negatives: It is a beautiful day today.
It was painted by a famous artist.

can_do_statement: Can use 'that of' and 'those of' as a possessive form, in formal and professional contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Formal comparison avoiding repetition of the head noun
ontology.pedagogical_hook: that of / those of

positives: Their approach is quite different from that of their competitors.
The opinions expressed do not reflect those of the general population.
negatives: I am not sure of that.
Those of us who were there know the truth.

can_do_statement: Can use pronouns 'none' to substitute for subject and object pronouns. ►  pronouns: substitution

ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'none' independently to replace a noun

positives: As for disadvantages, I see none.
Problems? None.
negatives: None of them are here.
I see none of the signs.

can_do_statement: Can use 'few', 'many', 'most', 'others' to refer to people in formal written contexts, often reports or surveys.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'few', 'many', 'most', 'others' as standalone subjects referring to people

positives: Few denied that it was thrilling.
Many express their satisfaction.
negatives: Few people denied it.
Many students express their satisfaction.

can_do_statement: Can use 'some of', 'many of' to modify relative pronouns in a relative clause.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'some of' or 'many of' before 'which' or 'whom'

positives: I saw his new inventions, some of which were enormous.
I have many friends, many of whom are active in sports.
negatives: Some of them were enormous.
Many of the people are active.

can_do_statement: Can modify 'few' and 'many' with 'very', 'too', 'so' as intensifiers.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: modifying 'few' and 'many' (as standalone pronouns) with 'very', 'too', or 'so'

positives: There were too many.
Very few managed to survive.
negatives: There were too many people.
Very few students survived.

can_do_statement: Can use 'none' as a pronoun. ►  determiners: quantity  ►  pronouns: quantity

ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'none' to mean 'not any'

positives: Then I searched for a Coca-Cola, but I found none.
We expected a social programme but there was none.
negatives: None of them are here.
They were none the wiser.

can_do_statement: Can use 'anything' in an ellipted clause, ('if there is anything …').

ontology.mental_model: Open condition or request without explicit condition.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Dropping 'if there is' before 'anything'.

positives: Anything you need, just ask.
Anything else you want, let me know.
negatives: If there is anything you need, ask me.
I don't need anything.

can_do_statement: Can use 'anything' with post-modifiers to form complex noun phrases as subjects with a singular verb, to give focus.

ontology.mental_model: Focusing on any entity that meets specific conditions.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'anything' modified by a phrase or clause as the subject.

positives: Anything that makes you happy is fine.
Anything to eat will do.
negatives: I don't have anything that makes you happy.
He needs anything to eat.

can_do_statement: Can use 'each' (+ noun or pronoun) as subject followed by 'the other(s)' a complement of a preposition, to refer to two related things. ► pronouns: quantity

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'each' as subject and 'the other(s)' as prepositional complement

positives: Each person could be a help to the other.
Each of them differs slightly from the others.
negatives: Each of them admires the other's intelligence.
They each helped the others.

can_do_statement: Can form alternative questions with two clauses and ellipsis in the second clause, often as a hedging device.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using ellipted modals after 'or' for polite suggestions

positives: Maybe you could hand out toys or show a movie?
Perhaps we should leave early or stay a bit longer?
negatives: Could you bring tea or coffee?
Will you go to the store or will you stay home?

can_do_statement: Can form alternative questions using an extreme alternative to give greater pragmatic force.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using extreme alternatives for rhetorical effect

positives: Is this new industry a blessing for the region or the exact opposite?
Are we making progress or nothing at all?
negatives: Should we take this route or the other one?
Do you want a large pizza or a small one?

can_do_statement: Can use affirmative and negative forms of question tags with 'there' + 'be'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'is/are there' in question tags

positives: As you put it that way, there isn't much of a difference with our time, is there?
But there is always something you can improve, isn't there?
negatives: There isn't any milk left in the fridge.
Is there anyone who can help me?

can_do_statement: Can use 'wh-'questions as a focusing device, often in a narrative or argument.

ontology.mental_model: Using rhetorical or structural questions to guide the listener's attention in discourse
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To structure an argument or narrative by posing a question before answering it

positives: But what are the alternatives?
So what makes a good present?
negatives: What are the alternatives?
I wonder what makes a good present.

can_do_statement: Can use verb + particle + preposition, where the preposition is separated from its complement. ► Prepositions

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Notice how the final preposition hangs at the end, waiting for context.

positives: Anyway, let me tell you what ideas I came up with.
This is something you will have to look out for.
negatives: I came up with a great idea yesterday.
I look out for him every day.

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of phrasal verbs + object pronoun + particle.

ontology.mental_model: Manipulating specific entities with advanced phrasal verbs.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Putting a pronoun in the middle of an advanced phrasal verb.

positives: I went to check them out last week.
I tried to clean it up.
negatives: Check out the new store.
Clean up the kitchen.

guideword: FORM/USE: VERBS OF SENSES + OBJECT + INFINITIVE
can_do_statement: Can use some verbs connected with the senses + direct object + infinitive without 'to' emphasising a complete action.

ontology.mental_model: Emphasizing a complete action through sensory perception.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Describing a full event you witnessed.

positives: I would like to see it develop.
It is common to hear people talk about it.
negatives: I saw him running away.
I like to hear the music.

can_do_statement: Can use a list of adjectives in ellipted clauses before and after a noun, to give focus. ► focus

ontology.mental_model: fronted attribute list spotlights the referent
ontology.pedagogical_hook: praise first, name second

negatives: He was imaginative, kind and friendly.
He walked in tall and dark.
positives: Imaginative, kind and friendly, he was loved.
Tall, dark and handsome, he walked in.

can_do_statement: Can combine more complex, lengthy strings of adjectives, joining the last two adjectives with 'and'.

ontology.mental_model: long attribute chain closed by and
ontology.pedagogical_hook: build the long list cleanly

positives: The house was big, bright and beautiful.
The problem is complex, difficult and confusing.
negatives: Stop and Shop and Dollar Tree or Family Dollar.
Between husband and wife, domestic violence.

can_do_statement: Can use 'no' / 'not any' with comparative adjectives to limit the scale of comparison. ► comparative clauses

ontology.mental_model: no caps the scale at zero difference
ontology.pedagogical_hook: deny the gap entirely

positives: It is no better than before.
I am not any happier here.
negatives: It is not better.
Not older, it's like 45.

can_do_statement: Can use 'not that much' to modify comparative adjectives to a small degree. ► comparative clauses

ontology.mental_model: not that much shrinks the distance under scrutiny
ontology.pedagogical_hook: understate the gap

negatives: I don't have that much money.
It is much better.
positives: She is not that much older than I am.
The trip was not that much worse than driving.

can_do_statement: Can use adjectives in 'as … as' and 'so … that' in comparative structures. ► comparative clauses

ontology.mental_model: as/so inserts the adjective between scale and article
ontology.pedagogical_hook: adjective splits as and a

negatives: He is as tall as his brother.
It was so big that we laughed.
positives: Our debates do not draw as large a number of students as the guest appearances.
He had so strong a shock that he never spoke of it.

can_do_statement: Can use an increasing range of adjectives before a noun to express intensity.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: intensifier + adjective + noun — push the quality word to the upper extreme before the entity
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker escalates a quality to its extreme

positives: The major problem concerns the exam.
It was a complete disaster for the team.
negatives: I went to the cinema yesterday.
She left her book here.

can_do_statement: Can use 'the slightest', 'the faintest' with a specific range of nouns to express the least amount possible, most frequently following a negative verb form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: the slightest / the faintest + noun — name the tiniest margin of a thing

positives: I don't have the slightest idea what you mean.
There wasn't the faintest trace of evidence.
negatives: I have a slight idea.
There is a faint trace of light.

sub_category: adverbs and adverb phrases: types and meanings
can_do_statement: Can use adverbs mid clause, to distance the writer from what they are saying.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: allegedly / supposedly / reportedly / presumably — disclaim responsibility for the assertion

positives: It allegedly happened yesterday.
The suspect supposedly left the scene.
negatives: I only remember the it's called I Am Richard.
Apparently he didn't know.

can_do_statement: Can use adverbs in mid position, to distance the writer from what they are saying.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: allegedly / supposedly / reportedly / theoretically / arguably / presumably — slot distancing adverbs medially
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker maximum-distance from the proposition mid-clause

positives: It is technically possible.
She has practically finished the report.
negatives: Apparently I am interested to see.
Supposedly they do not have sentiment.

can_do_statement: Can use 'hardly' in front position followed by an inverted subject and verb, to give focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Hardly + aux + subject + verb — flip the clause around 'hardly' for dramatic foregrounding
ontology.agency_or_distance: speaker front-loads 'hardly' and rearranges the clause for emphasis

positives: Hardly had he reached his front door when he heard the phone ringing.
Hardly had she finished her complaints when the bell rang.
negatives: I hardly ever go there.
Hardly anything happened that afternoon.

can_do_statement: Can form adverb phrases with modifiers before, and complements after, adverbs.

ontology.mental_model: Enveloping adverbs in pre- and post-modifiers for absolute precision
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Forming complex adverb phrases with both preceding and following modifiers

positives: To work almost exclusively for their own interests.
It was so completely in harmony with the sun.
negatives: To work exclusively for their own interests.
It was completely in harmony with the sun.

can_do_statement: Can use 'so' + adjective + 'as' + 'to'-infinitive clause, usually in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Connecting a state to an extreme consequence.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Formal 'so ... as to' construction.

positives: Travellers should not be so ignorant as to think they can understand.
Should I be so fortunate as to win the scholarship...
negatives: It is so good as this one.
He spoke so as to be heard.

can_do_statement: Can use 'as if' + non-finite clause to introduce a second clause as a comparison.

ontology.mental_model: Drawing a comparison to an implied action.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'as if' followed by a non-finite clause.

positives: She closed her eyes as if to push those thoughts away.
I was so frightened that my heart was beating like crazy as if trying to leave my body.
negatives: She acts as if she knows.
As if he was looking for something.

can_do_statement: Can combine a negative clause with an inverted clause with 'nor', to give focus.

ontology.mental_model: Addition of a second negative point
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'nor' after a negative sentence

positives: That night Kevin did not sleep; nor did Kristin.
Her diary was never found, nor was Juliette.
negatives: They neither got married nor had children.
I have neither time nor money.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'LET' + THIRD PERSON PRONOUN, DEVOLVING RESPONSIBILITY
can_do_statement: Can use an imperative clause with 'let' + 'him/her/them' + base form of a main verb, to devolve responsibility.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Hands Off — withdrawing control entirely and ceding the outcome to another agent.

positives: Let them be.
Let them find their own food.
negatives: Let them have more free time.
Let him decide what to do.

can_do_statement: Can use you with an imperative form to make an instruction stronger.

positives: Don't you ever do that again!
Don't you dare forget about us!
negatives: Don't you know the answer?
Don't you like chocolate ice cream?

can_do_statement: Can use 'How' + clause.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'How' directly followed by a subject and verb.

positives: How I love the smell of home!
How she wishes things were different.
negatives: How are you?
How exciting!

can_do_statement: Can use 'How' + adverb + clause.

ontology.mental_model: Emphasizing the manner of an action.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'How' + adverb to start an exclamation.

positives: How beautifully she sang.
How differently we were brought up.
negatives: How I love that.
How exciting!

can_do_statement: Can use 'Were' + pronoun + 'to' infinitive to introduce a condition, in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Were I to...

positives: Were we to give them this opportunity, it would be a great advantage.
Were they to be paid a sufficient sum, they would agree.
negatives: We were to meet at noon.
If we were to go, we would need money.

can_do_statement: Can use non-finite clauses after subordinating conjunctions '(although, though)', to express contrast.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: although/though + past participle or adjective

positives: Although committed to her job, she maintains social contacts.
Jack, though disappointed, respects the result.
negatives: Although she was committed to her job, she quit.
Though he is tired, he continues.

guideword: FORM/USE: INVERTED PAST PERFECT, IMAGINED PAST
can_do_statement: Can use past perfect +  inverted subject, and a modal verb + 'have' + '-ed' in the main clause  to talk about imagined situations in the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'Had' + subject to mean 'If subject had'.

positives: Had he been more experienced he would have known.
Had I known, I would have studied harder.
negatives: He had been there before.
I would have gone if I had known.

guideword: USE: INVERTED 'SHOULD', FUTURE, POSSIBLE OUTCOME, FORMAL, POLITE
can_do_statement: Can use inverted 'should', + 'would' in the main clause to talk about possible future outcomes, in polite or formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'Should' + subject to mean 'If subject should'.

positives: Should we win your prize we would like to build a new school.
Should you fail to do so, we would have no choice.
negatives: We should win your prize.
You should fail to do so.

can_do_statement: Can use 'Were it not for' + noun phrase to introduce conditions in formal contexts. ► past simple

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'Were it not for' to mean 'If it were not for'.

positives: Were it not for my university, I would give up this class immediately.
In fact, were it not for that reason, Laura would have accepted.
negatives: It was not for me.
They were not for sale.

can_do_statement: Can use 'were' with an inverted subject + 'to' infinitive, to introduce conditions in formal contexts. ► past simple

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'Were' + subject + 'to' to mean 'If subject were to'.

positives: Were I to win this travel scholarship, I would be happy.
Were you to compare people's views, you would find similarities.
negatives: We were to go to the store.
They were to be married.

can_do_statement: Can use conditional subordinate clauses with a range of conjunctions ('so long as', 'on condition that', 'in the event that') with past, present or future reference.|

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'so long as' or 'on condition that'.

positives: They can attend whichever university they desire so long as they qualify.
I was allowed to go out on condition that my parents knew.
negatives: It was so long as a trip.
The condition that he has is bad.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'IF IT WERE NOT FOR', FORMAL
can_do_statement: Can use 'If it weren’t / were not for' + noun phrase to introduce conditions in formal contexts. ► past simple

ontology.mental_model: Counterfactual condition based on the absence of something
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Expressing how things would be different without a specific factor

positives: If it weren't for that boy, I would have failed.
If it were not for his determination, he would have resigned.
negatives: I wonder if it were not meant to be.
They asked if it were not for me, but for him.

can_do_statement: Can use 'If it were' + 'to-' infinitive to introduce conditions in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'were to' for unlikely future scenarios

positives: If it were to be published, the first issue would include an introduction.
It will need planning if it were to succeed.
negatives: I asked if it were too late.
If it were true, I would know.

can_do_statement: Can use 'whether or not' to introduce conditions in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Condition that is irrelevant to the outcome
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Expressing that something is true in either case

positives: Whether or not the visitors should imitate local customs is debatable.
Whether or not it is better to educate boys and girls separately is widely discussed.
negatives: I don't know whether to go or not.
Whether he comes or not is unknown.

can_do_statement: Can use 'Neither' or 'Nor' + inverted auxiliary or 'be' + subject to add to a previous related negative clause, to focus on an additional negative factor.

ontology.mental_model: Appending a structurally inverted negative extension to a prior negation.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Follow a negative sentence with 'Neither' or 'Nor', then flip the subject and auxiliary to add another negative.

positives: I did not see the movie. Neither did my friend.
He is not ready. Nor is she.
negatives: Neither John nor Mary was there.
I like neither of them.

can_do_statement: Can use 'And yet' to combine sentences to introduce a contrast, often unexpected, sometimes in a formal context.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: sentence-initial unexpected contrast

positives: It was raining. And yet, we went out.
And yet the manager forgave me.
negatives: I haven't gone out and played yet.
The host family was carefully selected, yet it was four miles away.

can_do_statement: Can use 'in that' as a subordinating conjunction, to give greater in-depth explanation, often in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: in that for explanation

positives: Nowadays it is widely argued that professional sports are damaging to people's health in that they involve gruelling training sessions.
It's often said that nowadays people must be proud of medical advances, in that life is getting considerably longer.
negatives: I'll be in that room.
She lives in that house.

can_do_statement: Can use 'this' with nouns and noun phrases in a narrative to create a sense of immediacy.

ontology.mental_model: Creating narrative immediacy through reference to specific entities.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Bringing the listener into the story with 'this' character or event.

positives: Then we saw this woman running away.
And this man just stared at me.
negatives: We will do it in this time.
this guy wants to control this power

can_do_statement: Can use 'this' + noun + 'of' + possessive pronoun to highlight something, often in a positive way.

ontology.mental_model: Highlighting a specific noun phrase through a demonstrative and a possessive structure.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasizing a trait by using 'this [noun] of [possessive]'.

positives: This rare talent of theirs is used for public pleasure.
This characteristic of his is shown in every situation.
negatives: This is his rare talent.
His characteristic is shown everywhere.

can_do_statement: Can use 'that' and 'those' to convey emotional distance, often to express disapproval.

ontology.mental_model: Distancing oneself from a concept or behaviour.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'that' or 'those' for emotional distance or disapproval.

positives: I would never accept that sort of treatment.
Why do we listen to those so-called heroes?
negatives: I have that sort in my collection already.
Those are my friends.

guideword: FORM: SINGULAR NOUN ENDING IN 'S' + APOSTROPHE
can_do_statement: Can use an apostrophe after singular nouns ending in 's', to indicate possession.

ontology.mental_model: Mapping possession, quantification, or specific reference to an entity.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Identifying the scope or owner of a noun phrase.

positives: We must keep the series' aspects the same.
I drove James' car to the store.
negatives: My parents' house is nearby.
The dog's bowl is empty.

can_do_statement: Can use two possessive ''s' constructions in the same noun phrase.

ontology.mental_model: Mapping possession, quantification, or specific reference to an entity.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Identifying the scope or owner of a noun phrase.

positives: They were in Ann's mother's albums.
We went to Emily's grandmother's house.
negatives: Ann's mother is nice.
The cat's toy is under the dog's bed.

can_do_statement: Can use ''s' without a following noun when the noun has already been mentioned or is obvious in the context.

ontology.mental_model: Mapping possession, quantification, or specific reference to an entity.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Identifying the scope or owner of a noun phrase.

positives: Olivia's experiences are probably the narrator's.
The empty account was my friend's.
negatives: My friend's car is empty.
Olivia's experience was fun.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'MANY A' WITH SINGULAR NOUNS, FOR FOCUS
can_do_statement: Can use 'many a' or 'many an' + singular noun for emphasis and focus.

ontology.mental_model: Literary or emphatic expression of multitude using singular forms.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'many a time' or 'many an issue'.

positives: We have climbed many a mountain.
It has raised many an issue.
negatives: Many people were there.
I don't have many apples.

can_do_statement: Can use 'Not a' + noun with a passive verb or inverted auxiliary and subject for focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasizing absence completely

positives: Not a word was spoken during the entire meeting.
Not a cloud could be seen in the sky.
negatives: It is not a good idea to leave now.
This is not a drill.

can_do_statement: Can use 'The' + premodifier + 'thing, fact, point, problem or reason' + 'is (that)' for focus.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Adding color to the focal point

positives: The sad thing about it was that he never returned.
The main problem is that we have no backup.
negatives: It was a very sad thing to witness.
We discussed the main problem at length.

can_do_statement: Can use 'How', 'Why', or 'Where' cleft clauses as subject, for focus

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Making circumstances the subject

positives: How they influenced my life is hard to tell.
Where he had gone to was a complete mystery.
negatives: Do you know how they influenced my life?
Where had he gone after the party?

can_do_statement: Can use 'It' + 'be' + noun + 'that' clause for focus.

ontology.mental_model: Highlighting a specific entity in discourse by placing it in a cleft structure
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use 'It is X that/who...' to emphasize the importance of X.

positives: It was Paul who stole the money.
It is this silence that gives me the impression of togetherness.
negatives: It is clear that he is absolutely right.
I know the man who is standing there.

can_do_statement: Can use more than one fixed expression in the front position for added focus.

ontology.mental_model: Stacking discourse markers for heavy emphasis at the beginning of a sentence
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use multiple fixed expressions like 'All in all, taking everything into account' to strongly frame your point.

positives: All in all, taking everything into account, it was a great experience.
All in all, taking everything into account, we decided to stay.
negatives: All in all it was quite good.
Taking everything into account, it was fine.

can_do_statement: Can use the simple past form of 'be' + 'due to' to talk about scheduled events in the future from a point in the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: talking about something formally planned in the past

positives: My plane was due to leave in 40 minutes.
The factory was due to be built near the lake.
negatives: The flight is due to arrive at noon.
His success was due to hard work.

can_do_statement: Can use the future perfect continuous to make assumptions about the present.

ontology.mental_model: assumption about an ongoing present state
ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'will have been doing' to guess what is happening now

positives: I suppose you will have been studying very hard for this exam.
I imagine they'll have been waiting for hours.
negatives: By tomorrow, I will have been working for ten years.
I guess he will have finished it by now.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form of the future perfect simple.

ontology.mental_model: asking about a completed event before a future time
ontology.pedagogical_hook: asking if something will be finished by a future time

positives: Will he have changed?
Won't they have finished by tomorrow?
negatives: He will have changed.
Will he change by tomorrow?

can_do_statement: Can use 'shall' to talk about long-term intentions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'shall' with adverbs like 'never' or 'always' for long-term commitments.

positives: This way I shall never lose hope.
I shall always remember it as the city of lights.
negatives: I shall go to the store today.
We shall meet at noon.

can_do_statement: Can use 'shall' to make predictions, usually in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using future constructs to indicate forthcoming actions or states.
ontology.agency_or_distance: Agency via intention; Distance via forward-looking temporal projection.

positives: We shall meet in November.
I hope we shall soon discover the truth.
negatives: He demanded that she shall not pass.
Shall we dance?

can_do_statement: Can use 'be' + 'going to' with a wide range of adverbs before the main verb.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using future constructs to indicate forthcoming actions or states.
ontology.agency_or_distance: Agency via intention; Distance via forward-looking temporal projection.

positives: I'm going to still live here.
I am going to briefly introduce the activities.
negatives: I am going to live here still.
He is going to introduce it briefly.

can_do_statement: Can use the present simple with 'only when' (followed by 'will' and inverted subject) to refer to the future.

ontology.mental_model: exclusive condition for a future event
ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'only when' + present simple + will inversion

positives: Only when we understand that, will we be able to live in better societies.
Only when the rain stops will we go out.
negatives: Only when we understood that, did we help.
It is only when it rains.

can_do_statement: Can use 'how can' to reflect, through rhetorical questions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'how can' for reflections

positives: And how can we improve if we are not allowed to make mistakes?
But how can each of us stay fit in this world?
negatives: How can I help you?
I asked him how he can run so fast.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form 'didn't dare' + infinitive without 'to' to talk about not being brave enough to do something.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Expressing fear of doing something

positives: She didn't dare look back at the explosion.
They didn't dare say a word during the meeting.
negatives: I didn't dare to dream about winning.
He didn't dare me to do it.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be' + 'not' + adjective + 'to' + infinitive.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be not adjective to infinitive

positives: You are not likely to win.
She isn't expected to come.
negatives: He is not ready for you.
We are not trying to leave.

can_do_statement: Can use 'be' + adjective + 'not' + 'to' + infinitive for emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: be adjective not to

positives: We are determined not to fail.
They are obliged not to tell anyone.
negatives: I am not to blame.
She promised not to go.

can_do_statement: Can use present and past forms of 'have to' + '-ed' to talk about obligations in the past.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: past obligation with have to have

positives: You had to have finished the test before leaving.
She has to have passed the exam to apply.
negatives: I have to leave now.
They had to go home.

can_do_statement: Can use a range of present and past forms of 'have (got) to' to talk about deductions and conclusions.  ► must  ► had to

ontology.pedagogical_hook: have got to for deduction

positives: It has got to be a mistake.
There had to be a reason for this.
negatives: I have got to go now.
We have to finish this project.

can_do_statement: Can use 'have to have' + '-ed'.

ontology.mental_model: obligation situated in the past perfective
ontology.pedagogical_hook: have to have + past participle

positives: You have to have lived there to understand.
They have to have finished by now.
negatives: I have to have a coffee.
We had to go home.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may as well' to talk about what we think is the easiest or most logical course of action, often when we cannot see a better alternative or when it will not spoil the situation if you do that thing. ► might

ontology.mental_model: Accepting the most logical course of action
ontology.pedagogical_hook: When there's no better alternative, you can say you 'may as well' do something.

positives: After all, you may as well know.
I may as well see the other things.
negatives: He may do as well as she did.
She may well win the race.

can_do_statement: Can use 'it may be' + '-ed' that as a hedging device when drawing conclusions and summarising, particularly in academic contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: In academic writing, use 'it may be argued that' to soften your statements.

positives: It may be concluded that their ultimate aim remains unchanged.
It may be argued that a child's academic success is crucial.
negatives: It may be that he is right.
The car may be parked there.

can_do_statement: Can use 'may' in a subordinate clause expressing concession with 'however', 'whatever', 'whoever' … + 'it or this may be or seem'.

ontology.mental_model: Conceding a point regardless of conditions
ontology.pedagogical_hook: To say that something is true no matter what, use 'whatever it may be' or 'however it may seem'.

positives: However small it may be, I love it.
People enjoy what they are doing whatever it may be.
negatives: However, it may be true.
Whatever you do, you may be happy.

can_do_statement: Can use 'try as I might' for emphasis at the beginning of a sentence.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasis of effort

positives: Try as I might, I couldn't open the jar.
Try as I might, I just don't understand it.
negatives: I will try as I might to help.
He can try, as I might also do.

can_do_statement: Can use 'might as well', mostly to talk about or suggest what we think is the easiest or most logical course of action, often when we cannot see a better alternative. ► 'may'

ontology.mental_model: Suggesting the logical course of action
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Logical suggestions

positives: We might as well go home.
You might as well ask him.
negatives: He might as a consequence be late.
He might go as well.

can_do_statement: Can use ellipted 'must have' + '-ed' without a subject. ► ellipsis

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Speculating on the past (ellipsis)

positives: Must have fallen out of a car, or something.
Must have gone to the shop already.
negatives: He must have fallen out of the bed.
You must have forgotten the keys again.

can_do_statement: Can use 'must not have been' (especially with 'easy').

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Speculating negatively on the past

positives: It must not have been easy for him.
It mustn't have been more than an hour.
negatives: It must not have done much damage.
He must not have seen it coming.

can_do_statement: Can use 'must' with a wide range of adverbs in the normal mid position after the modal verb. ► adverbs|

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasizing statements

positives: There must certainly be other solutions.
Our town must clearly use this area.
negatives: You absolutely must read this book.
They clearly must state their terms.

can_do_statement: Can invert 'must' and the subject after negative phrases, e.g. 'not only', 'never', 'nor', to change the focus and give prominence/emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Formal emphasis

positives: Not only must you study hard, but also keep studying.
Nor must we overlook the human qualities.
negatives: You must not only read but understand.
We never must forget what happened.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Inversion with 'need' instead of 'do'

positives: Need you ask me again?
Need I say more about it?
negatives: Do you need to ask me?
I need you to stay here.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form rhetorically in discussion, typically in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: Rhetorical questioning to emphasize a point
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using modal 'need' question to imply the answer is obvious

positives: Need I go on with this story?
Need you work in this way?
negatives: I need you to work harder.
Do I need to go on?

can_do_statement: Can use 'oughtn't' (without 'to') + verb.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Dropping 'to' after 'oughtn't'

positives: You oughtn't miss it for the world!
She oughtn't ever speak to him like that.
negatives: You oughtn't to miss it.
You ought not to go.

can_do_statement: Can use 'ought' + subject + 'not to' + verb to form (rhetorical) questions, often in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Inverting 'ought' with subject followed by 'not to'

positives: Ought we not to learn from the mistakes of the past?
Ought they not to stay here?
negatives: Ought we to learn from this?
Should we not learn from the past?

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form 'ought not to'.

ontology.mental_model: Advisability or mild obligation, explicitly negated.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: When negating 'ought to', place 'not' between 'ought' and 'to'.
ontology.agency_or_distance: High modal distance; formal negative advice.

positives: We ought not to forget this.
There ought not to be a gap here.
negatives: We ought to go.
You should not do that.

can_do_statement: Can use 'shall' in the main clause after an 'if-' clause  ► conditionals

ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'If ... shall ...' for conditional outcomes.

positives: If it rains, we shall stay inside.
If we fail, they shall win.
negatives: We shall go to the store.
If it rains, we will stay.

can_do_statement: Can use 'shall' to make predictions.

ontology.mental_model: Stating expected future state based on current evidence.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'Shall' to predict what will happen.

positives: Our town shall have financial benefits.
We shall probably see a difference.
negatives: Shall we go?
I shall do the dishes.

can_do_statement: Can use 'as' + pronoun + 'used to' … to add background to a narrative, often to highlight something unusual.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Narrative backgrounding

positives: She had gone out for a walk in the woods as she used to do every Sunday.
He proposed to her, old flabby Nellie as he used to call her.
negatives: I used to play there as a kid.
As a teenager I used to be very sociable.

can_do_statement: Can use negative form 'used not to'

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Rare negative past habit

positives: I used not to do my homework.
As a teenager I used not to be very sociable.
negatives: I didn't use to play.
I am not used to the cold.

can_do_statement: Can use 'will' to talk about general behaviour, often disapprovingly.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'what [noun] will do' for characteristic behavior

positives: You know what children will do in these situations.
I cannot predict what people will do next!
negatives: I will do it tomorrow morning.
What do you want to do?

can_do_statement: Can use a wide range of adverbs with 'would', including 'undoubtedly', 'possibly', 'normally', 'personally', 'eventually', 'obviously', 'significantly', 'inevitably'. ► adverbs

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'would undoubtedly', 'would significantly' for precision.

positives: The construction would undoubtedly contribute.
It would significantly increase membership.
negatives: It is undoubtedly true.
I would really increase it.

can_do_statement: Can use adverbs expressing certainty as short responses.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Responding forcefully with single adverbs

positives: Do I agree with this statement? Definitely.
Will you join us? Certainly.
negatives: I will definitely join you.
She is certainly right.

can_do_statement: Can use 'couldn’t have' + '-ed' to speculate about the past.

ontology.mental_model: Agent uses a negative past modal to assert strong improbability or impossibility of a past event.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Saying something was impossible in the past
ontology.agency_or_distance: Distance: stepping back to firmly deduce a negative past conclusion

positives: Surely I couldn't have left it on my seat.
her mother couldn't have hidden it there just like that.
negatives: I couldn't help it.
It could have been worse.

can_do_statement: Can use 'not a' + noun, often with a following  passive structure, for emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasizing absence with not a

positives: Not a single noise could be heard from inside.
Not a single member of the group would have imagined that.
negatives: It is not a good idea.
This is not a toy.

can_do_statement: Can use a negative imperative form with 'you' to give a warning or reprimand.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using Don't you for strong warnings

positives: Don't you ever do that again!
Don't you dare forget me!
negatives: Why don't you come with us?
If you don't, you will regret it.

can_do_statement: Can use 'Neither' or 'Nor' + with 'do' or 'be' + inverted subject to add to a previous related negative clause, to focus on an additional negative factor.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Adding negative points with neither or nor and inversion

positives: Nor is it possible to watch television peacefully.
Neither did I oppose her need to get new clothes.
negatives: Neither option is viable right now.
I want neither of those choices.

can_do_statement: Can use 'in the least' after a negative form for emphasis.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasizing negation with in the least

positives: She has lost her brother but that does not discourage her in the least.
The director is not in the least interested.
negatives: He is the least interesting person I know.
At the very least, we should try.

guideword: FORM: COMPLEX NOUN PHRASES WITH 'LITTLE OR NO'  + NOUN
can_do_statement: Can form complex noun phrases with 'little or no' + noun.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: To emphasize that something is almost non-existent, use 'little or no' before a noun.

positives: They have little or no spare time to relax.
These blockbusters have little or no artistic value.
negatives: They have little time to relax.
There is no artistic value here.

can_do_statement: Can use passive non-finite '-ing' perfect forms in subordinate clauses to give explanatory background information.

ontology.mental_model: Past completed action contextualizing current state.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'having been V3' as a clause.

positives: Having been taught the rules, we went home.
Not having been given orders, he left.
negatives: Having been to Paris is a great advantage.
Not having been to the store, we lacked food.

can_do_statement: Can use non-finite '-ing' perfect forms of the passive as the complement of prepositions.

ontology.mental_model: Prepositional object describing a past passive state.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using preposition + 'having been V3'.

positives: He got a reward for having been invited.
She entered without having been bidden to do so.
negatives: Having been given the gift, she smiled.
Not having been told, he was confused.

ontology.mental_model: Action ongoing from past to present receiving comment.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present perfect continuous passive.

positives: The problem has been being discussed a lot lately.
These roads have been being repaired for months.
negatives: We have been discussing the problem.
The problem has been discussed.

can_do_statement: Can use 'have' + object + infinitive without 'to' to talk about asking or causing someone to do something, often in formal contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Delegated action (have someone do something).

positives: We will have them review the document.
I had the mechanic fix my car yesterday.
negatives: I have them all in my collection.
I have to see him right now.

can_do_statement: Can use the past continuous with 'always' or 'constantly' to talk about repeated events which are undesired or uncontrolled.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Past continuous + always/constantly.

positives: I was constantly trying to balance my life.
He was always getting into trouble.
negatives: He was actually acting weird.
I was just watching TV.

can_do_statement: Can use the question form.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: had you been doing?

positives: What had he been doing that morning?
Had they been waiting for long?
negatives: What has he been doing that morning?
He had been doing something.

guideword: FORM: FIXED EXPRESSIONS 'HAD IT NOT BEEN FOR', 'IF IT HADN'T BEEN FOR'
can_do_statement: Can use 'had it not been for' … and 'if it hadn’t been for' with a modal form for giving reasons.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Fixed idioms for attributing negative causality: 'had it not been for'

positives: Had it not been for the fact that I had already read the article, I would have thought otherwise.
If it hadn't been for my lack of knowledge, I wouldn't have been fired.
negatives: It had not been for sale at that time.
If it hasn't been for long, we can wait.

can_do_statement: Can use the negative form after 'if only' to express regret.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Negative regret: 'if only' + hadn't

positives: If only she had not changed, we would still be best friends.
If only I hadn't been that rude!
negatives: If only I had listened to you.
If only they wouldn't do that.

can_do_statement: Can invert the subject and affirmative auxiliary verb with 'hardly … when' to talk about something that happened immediately before something else, in formal contexts.

ontology.mental_model: An action occurs immediately before another one.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'hardly had' adds formal emphasis to the speed of succession between events.

positives: Hardly had she spoken these words when it dawned on the musician.
Hardly had the teacher arrived when the bell rang.
negatives: She had hardly spoken when the bell rang.
Hardly anyone noticed when we left the party.

can_do_statement: Can invert the subject and affirmative auxiliary verb with 'not only … but' as a focusing device. ► focus ► inversion

ontology.mental_model: Focalizing two related ongoing activities by fronting 'not only'.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Inversion: 'Not only have I been...' to heighten emphasis.

positives: Not only have I been wandering its streets, but I also know the people.
Not only has she recently been studying hard, but she also works.
negatives: I have not only been wandering its streets.
Not only had I been wandering its streets.

can_do_statement: Can use the present perfect simple to introduce news.

ontology.mental_model: Presenting recent events as new and highly relevant information to the listener.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Use the present perfect to deliver fresh news, like 'A new store has opened.'

positives: A new shopping centre has opened in our town.
The president has announced a new law.
negatives: A new shopping centre opened yesterday.
The president is announcing a new law.

can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous with verbs that are not usually used in this form to make statements and requests sound less direct.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present continuous with stative verbs for politeness

positives: I am hoping you might be able to help me.
We are wondering if you would like to come over.
negatives: I hope you can help me.
I wondered what he was doing.

guideword: FORM/USE: WITH ADVERBS OF INDEFINITE FREQUENCY
can_do_statement: Can use the present continuous with a wide range of adverbs of indefinite frequency, often to talk about surprising or undesirable situations or events.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Present continuous with advanced frequency adverbs

positives: They are persistently changing the rules of the game.
He is perpetually complaining about the weather.
negatives: They persistently change the rules of the game.
She is always complaining about the weather.

can_do_statement: Can use 'that … of' + possessive pronouns to express an attitude about someone or something, often in humorous or sarcastic contexts.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: That ... of + possessive pronoun

positives: You can park that precious jeep of yours.
I kept silent about that new girlfriend of his.
negatives: That is completely out of mine.
A friend of yours came by.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'his', with singular and plural reference, in subject and object position, and complement positions after 'be' and after prepositions.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possessive pronoun his

positives: His was not a happy childhood.
He was my confidant and I was his.
negatives: His childhood was not happy.
I saw his face.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'theirs', with singular and plural reference, in subject position.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possessive pronoun theirs as subject

positives: Theirs had always been a complicated relationship.
Beautiful dreams end, and theirs lasted until she left.
negatives: The responsibility is theirs.
Their relationship was complex.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronoun 'hers' with singular reference, in subject position.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Possessive pronoun hers as subject

positives: I packed my bag because hers was already packed.
She thought hers was a drab existence.
negatives: The packed bag is hers.
Her bag is already packed.

can_do_statement: Can use the possessive pronouns 'hers', 'theirs' and 'his' after noun + 'of'.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Noun + of theirs/hers/his

positives: She asked some old friends of hers.
He showed me a very old diary of his.
negatives: Some of his friends are coming.
One of their diaries was lost.

can_do_statement: Can use 'as for myself' as a discourse marker to introduce or focus on a personal opinion.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Introducing personal opinion

positives: As for myself, I prefer tea.
Well, as for myself, I agree.
negatives: I bought it as a gift for myself.
She works as hard for myself as for others.

can_do_statement: Can form a cleft construction beginning with 'it' to emphasise the subject of the main clause. ► clauses

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Emphasising with 'it is... who/that'

positives: It was my father who took all this away from me.
It is the blue one that I prefer.
negatives: It is hot today.
It was going to rain.

can_do_statement: Can use 'a lot' and 'much' as a subject pronouns. ► focus

ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'a lot' or 'much' independently as sentence subjects for focus

positives: A lot has changed.
Much has been said about this.
negatives: A lot of people changed.
I like it very much.

guideword: FORM/USE: 'MANY ARE THE' + NOUN, FOR FOCUS
can_do_statement: Can form complex noun phrases using an inverted form 'Many' + 'are' + noun phrase, followed by a relative clause, as a focusing device.  ► focus

ontology.pedagogical_hook: using 'Many are the...' for rhetorical focus

positives: Many are the causes which have led us here.
Many are the examples of children who hate reading.
negatives: There are many causes.
Many people are the leaders of the group.

can_do_statement: Can use 'The one(s) that' + clause in subject position, for focus. ► focus

ontology.pedagogical_hook: 'The one(s) that' for emphasizing a subject

positives: The one that impressed me a lot is the Chinese Lunar New Year Carnival.
The ones that wear clothes made by their mothers never seem to ask for much attention.
negatives: I liked the one that you bought.
He saw the ones that were red.

can_do_statement: Can use 'each' (+ noun or pronoun) as subject followed by 'the other(s)' as object , to refer to two related things. ► pronouns: quantity

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using 'each' as subject and 'the other(s)' as object

positives: Each of them admires the other's intelligence.
Each one is helping the others.
negatives: Each person could be a help to the other.
Each gave a gift to the other.

can_do_statement: Can form alternative questions with two or more clauses and ellipsis in the second or third clause.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using ellipsis in lists of clauses

positives: Do you enjoy reading, find it a waste of time or have an indifferent attitude to it?
Is it not better to take the television away or stop them going to the cinema?
negatives: Are you still with him or did you two break up?
Do you want apples, oranges or bananas?

can_do_statement: Can form negative questions with uncontracted 'not' to emphasise a point in an argument.

ontology.mental_model: Emphasising a point with uncontracted not
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Using uncontracted not for emphasis in negative questions

positives: Are we not supposed to be there, right?
Do you not understand?
negatives: We are not supposed to be there.
They do not know.

guideword: FORM: VERB + DIRECT OBJECT + PARTICLE + PREPOSITION + OBJECT
can_do_statement: Can use a direct object with some prepositional verbs as well as an object of the preposition.

ontology.pedagogical_hook: The object sits directly after the verb, splitting the verb from its particles.

positives: They can trust us or let us in on a secret.
Please don't put me up to this task.
negatives: Please let us in right now.
They decided to let us go.

can_do_statement: Can use 'would hate' + 'to' infinitive, for emphasis.

ontology.mental_model: Expressing a strong negative preference about a hypothetical situation.
ontology.pedagogical_hook: Saying you really wouldn't want something to happen.

positives: I would hate to see all that space go to waste.
I'd really hate to make the same mistakes.
negatives: I hate to do that.
I would like to see it.
